kind: algorithm
title: "Finite-budget thick and implicitly restarted Arnoldi with residual acceptance and locking"
status: draft

deps:

  - def-real-and-complex-givens-transformations
  - def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations
  - def-unshifted-and-shifted-qr-iteration-with-deflation-and-wilkinson-shift
  - prop-shifted-qr-preserves-upper-hessenberg-form
  - def-upper-hessenberg-and-real-symmetric-tridiagonal-matrices

  proof: not-applicable
verification:

sources:
  references:
    - title: "Yousef Saad, Numerical Methods for Large Eigenvalue Problems, second edition, §§7.3 and 8.1.3"
      url: "https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~saad/eig_book_2ndEd.pdf"
    - title: "Peter Arbenz, Lecture Notes on Solving Large Scale Eigenvalue Problems, §§11.2 and 11.7"
      url: "https://people.inf.ethz.ch/arbenz/ewp/Lnotes/lsevp.pdf"
---

## Definition

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $v\ne0$, and choose integers
$1\le r<m\le n$, a residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a restart budget
$N_{\max}\ge1$, and a restart mode `thick` or `implicit`. All operations
below are in exact arithmetic. The number $k$ of locked pairs is the number
of linearly independent locked vectors; it starts at zero. If a restart is
needed, a target rule may be supplied for thick mode and is required for an
implicit-mode restart after one or more pairs are locked. When invoked, it
must return $r-k$ current Ritz vectors independent modulo the span of all
locked vectors, or report `unavailable`; no rule, an unavailable selection,
or a wrong-size or dependent selection gives status `rank-loss`. For an implicit-mode
restart with no locked pairs, a shift rule supplies exactly $p=m-r$ complex
shifts for the current cycle or reports `unavailable`; an unavailable list or
a list of any other length gives status `shift-count-unavailable`. The shifts
may be chosen from unwanted Ritz values, but the procedure allows any
supplied list and asserts no convergence for an arbitrary schedule.

Initialize the restart counter $c=0$ before the first Arnoldi cycle. A cycle
consists of expanding the current Arnoldi basis to dimension $m$ or exact
breakdown, then computing Ritz pairs and testing their original residuals.
After the initial cycle in step 1, each restart in step 3 or 4 constructs the
next cycle. The output is the locked Ritz pairs, the current unlocked Ritz
pairs, and one of `converged`, `budget-exhausted`,
`invariant-subspace-breakdown`, `rank-loss`, `shift-count-unavailable`, or
`filtered-breakdown`.

1. Start with $v_1=v/\|v\|_2$, no locked pairs, and run fully reorthogonalized
   Arnoldi to dimension $m$, stopping earlier if the next Arnoldi residual is
   zero. Let $d$ be the number of basis columns actually constructed, so
   $d=m$ unless exact breakdown occurs earlier, and let $V_d,H_d$ be the
   resulting basis and projected matrix. Normalize every nonzero projected
   eigenvector $y$ of $H_d$ so $\|y\|_2=1$ and lift it to $u=V_dy$. Process
   the Ritz pairs in the order returned by the projected eigensolve. For each
   pair $(\theta,u)$, compute the original residual $r_u=Au-\theta u$
   directly (on a standard Arnoldi cycle without breakdown it may be
   evaluated by [[prop-ritz-residual-formula-for-an-arnoldi-ritz-pair]]).
   If $\|r_u\|_2\le\tau$ and adding $u$ increases the exact rank of the
   locked-vector matrix, append $(\theta,u)$ to the locked outputs and
   increment $k$. A
   residual-accepted vector in the span of the locked vectors is not counted
   or appended again. Locked vectors are retained as a subspace at every
   later restart. If $k\ge r$, return `converged`.

2. If the projected Arnoldi space is exactly invariant and fewer than $r$
   pairs are locked, return `invariant-subspace-breakdown`. If the restart
   counter satisfies $c=N_{\max}$, return `budget-exhausted`.

3. For a thick restart, or for an implicit-mode restart when $k>0$, invoke
   the target rule. Form a target block from every locked vector and the
   selected $r-k$ wanted Ritz vectors. For either block to be rank-revealing,
   use the following exact column-pivoted orthogonalization: start with an
   empty orthonormal block $Q$ and all input columns remaining. For each
   remaining column $y_j$, compute $c_j=y_j-Q(Q^*y_j)$. Choose a column with
   largest $\|c_j\|_2$, breaking ties by original column order. If the largest
   norm is zero, stop; otherwise append $c_j/\|c_j\|_2$ to $Q$ and remove that
   pivot column. The columns appended to $Q$ form an ordered orthonormal basis
   of the input range. Apply this procedure first to the target block; if it
   fails to retain all locked and selected directions, return `rank-loss`.
   With its resulting orthonormal basis $U$, compute the residual block
   $R_U=(I-UU^*)AU$. Apply the same orthogonalization to $R_U$ to obtain an
   ordered orthonormal basis $F$ of its range. If $U$ has $s$ columns, retain
   only the first $\min(\dim\operatorname{range}(R_U),m-s)$ columns of $F$,
   so $[U,F]$ has at most $m$ columns. Set the ordered basis to $[U,F]$ and a
   queue to its columns in order. While the basis has fewer than $m$ columns
   and the queue is nonempty, remove the first queued column $q$, compute
   $w=Aq$, and orthogonalize $w$ against every current basis column in two
   complete passes. If the residual is nonzero, normalize it, append it to
   the basis, and append the new column to the queue; if it is zero, continue
   with the remaining queue. If the queue empties before the basis has
   dimension $m$, the retained subspace is invariant; when fewer than $r$
   pairs are locked, return `invariant-subspace-breakdown`.

4. For an implicit restart with no locked pairs, set $p=m-r$ and request a
   shift list $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_p$ from the shift rule. If it reports
   `unavailable` or returns a list of the wrong length, return
   `shift-count-unavailable`.
   Starting from $AV_m=V_mH_m+\beta_m v_{m+1}e_m^*$, apply exact shifted QR
   steps to $H_m$ using the Givens transformations of
   [[def-real-and-complex-givens-transformations]] in top-down adjacent-row
   eliminations on pairs
   $(1,2),(2,3),\ldots,(m-1,m)$:
   $H_{j-1}-\mu_jI=Q_jR_j$ and $H_j=Q_j^*H_{j-1}Q_j=R_jQ_j+\mu_jI$.
   Put $Q=Q_1\cdots Q_p$, rotate $V_m$ by $Q$, retain its first $r$ columns,
   and continue Arnoldi to dimension $m$. If the polynomial
   $q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^p(z-\mu_j)$ annihilates the starting vector or the
   filtered Krylov space has dimension below $r$, return `filtered-breakdown`.

5. Increment the restart counter by setting $c\gets c+1$, recompute Ritz
   pairs and their original residuals, apply the acceptance rule in step 1,
   and return to step 2 unless a return status applies.
   No convergence is asserted for an arbitrary shift schedule. The residual
   acceptance test certifies only the computed residual size; it does not by
   itself give a forward eigenvalue bound for a nonnormal matrix.

id: thm-implicit-restart-polynomial-subspace-and-residual-identity
kind: theorem
title: "Exact implicit Arnoldi restart applies its shift polynomial and preserves an Arnoldi residual identity"
status: draft
origin: pipeline

sources:
  references:
    - title: "Yousef Saad, Numerical Methods for Large Eigenvalue Problems, second edition, §7.3"
      url: "https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~saad/eig_book_2ndEd.pdf"
    - title: "Peter Arbenz, Lecture Notes on Solving Large Scale Eigenvalue Problems, §11.2"
      url: "https://people.inf.ethz.ch/arbenz/ewp/Lnotes/lsevp.pdf"
---

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, and suppose an exact $m$-step Arnoldi
factorization without breakdown is
$$AV_m=V_mH_m+\beta_m v_{m+1}e_m^*,\qquad V_m^*V_m=I_m,$$
where $H_m$ is upper Hessenberg and $\beta_m>0$. Let $1\le r<m$,
$p=m-r$, and let $H_{j-1}-\mu_jI=Q_jR_j$ be exact shifted QR factorizations
using the ordered top-down adjacent-row Givens eliminations on pairs
$(1,2),(2,3),\ldots,(m-1,m)$, with $R_j$ upper triangular. Put
$$Q=Q_1\cdots Q_p,\qquad H^+=Q^*H_mQ,\qquad q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^p(z-\mu_j).$$
Assume $q(A)v_1\ne0$, the exact filtered Krylov space
$K_r(A,q(A)v_1)$ has dimension $r$, and $\rho\ne0$ in the factorization
$q(H_m)=QR$ with $R$ upper triangular. Then
$$\operatorname{range}(V_mQ(:,1:r))=K_r(A,q(A)v_1).$$
Writing $H_r^+=H^+(1:r,1:r)$, $h^+=H^+_{r+1,r}$, and
$$g=h^+V_mQe_{r+1}+\beta_m(e_m^*Qe_r)v_{m+1},$$
the truncated restart has the exact residual identity
$$AV_mQ(:,1:r)=V_mQ(:,1:r)H_r^++g e_r^*.$$
If $g\ne0$, then $v_{r+1}^+=g/\|g\|_2$ is orthogonal to the retained
columns and the new Arnoldi residual coefficient is $\beta_r^+=\|g\|_2$;
if $g=0$, the retained subspace is exactly invariant.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The no-breakdown Arnoldi factorization, dimensions and shifts in the
Statement, with the stated nonannihilation and filtered-dimension hypotheses.

[F1] [[thm-arnoldi-produces-an-orthonormal-krylov-basis-and-upper-hessenberg-factorization]]: before breakdown, $AQ_m=Q_{m+1}\bar H_m$, the Arnoldi vectors are orthonormal, and $H_m$ is upper Hessenberg; the present item writes this basis as $V_m$.

[F2] [[def-unshifted-and-shifted-qr-iteration-with-deflation-and-wilkinson-shift]]: a shifted QR step factors $H-\mu I=QR$ with $Q$ unitary and $R$ upper triangular, then sets $H_+=RQ+\mu I=Q^*HQ$.

[F3] [[prop-shifted-qr-preserves-upper-hessenberg-form]]: an exact shifted QR step built from adjacent-row Givens eliminations preserves upper Hessenberg form.

[F4] [[def-upper-hessenberg-and-real-symmetric-tridiagonal-matrices]]: upper Hessenberg means $H_{ij}=0$ whenever $i>j+1$.

[F5] [[def-real-and-complex-givens-transformations]] and [[def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations]]: the QR factorization in the Statement is formed by successive adjacent-row Givens rotations, with the unitary factor given by their ordered product.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $0\le j\le m-1$, $A^jv_1=V_mH_m^je_1$: the claim holds at $j=0$, and if it holds at $j<m-1$, [F1] gives $A^{j+1}v_1=V_mH_m^{j+1}e_1+\beta_m v_{m+1}e_m^*H_m^je_1$. By [F4], $H_m^je_1$ is supported in rows $1$ through $j+1$, so $e_m^*H_m^je_1=0$ when $j<m-1$; induction proves the identity through degree $m-1$. [F1, F4, algebra]

2.1 Since $\deg q=p<m$, step 1.1 gives $q(A)v_1=V_mq(H_m)e_1$. Put $P_j=Q_1\cdots Q_j$ and $P_0=I$; the cumulative similarities give $H_{j-1}=P_{j-1}^*H_mP_{j-1}$. Thus $H_m-\mu_jI=P_{j-1}(H_{j-1}-\mu_jI)P_{j-1}^*=P_{j-1}Q_jR_jP_{j-1}^*=P_jR_jP_{j-1}^*$. Because scalar factors commute, order the product as $q(H_m)=(H_m-\mu_pI)\cdots(H_m-\mu_1I)$; substituting these factorizations cancels every adjacent $P_{j-1}^*P_{j-1}$ and gives $q(H_m)=P_p(R_p\cdots R_1)=QR$. The product $R_p\cdots R_1$ is upper triangular, and $Re_1=\rho e_1$, so $q(A)v_1=\rho V_mQe_1$. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $0\le j<r$, $p+j\le m-1$, so applying step 1.1 to each monomial of $z^jq(z)$ gives $A^jq(A)v_1=V_mH_m^jq(H_m)e_1=\rho V_mQ(H^+)^je_1$. By [F3], $H^+$ is upper Hessenberg, so $(H^+)^je_1$ is supported in its first $j+1$ coordinates and the resulting vector lies in $\operatorname{range}(V_mQ(:,1:r))$. Thus $K_r(A,q(A)v_1)$ is contained in the retained range; both have dimension $r$, the former by hypothesis and the latter because $V_mQ$ has orthonormal columns, so they are equal. [given, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 In each shifted QR step the top-down left eliminations use row pairs $(1,2),(2,3),\ldots,(m-1,m)$; by [F5] the unitary factor is the ordered product of their adjoints. In $Q_i e_j$, rotations with index greater than $j$ act first and fix $e_j$, rotation $j$ adds at most row $j+1$, and rotations with smaller indices add only rows less than $j$; by [F4], each $Q_i$ is upper Hessenberg. If $C$ has lower bandwidth $a$ and $D$ lower bandwidth $b$, a nonzero term in $(CD)_{ij}=\sum_k C_{ik}D_{kj}$ requires $k\ge i-a$ and $k\le j+b$, so $CD$ has lower bandwidth at most $a+b$. Hence $Q=Q_1\cdots Q_p$ has lower bandwidth $p$ and $e_m^*Qe_j=0$ for $j<m-p=r$. Multiplying the Arnoldi factorization in [F1] by $Q$ yields $AV_mQ=V_mQH^++\beta_m v_{m+1}e_m^*Q$; since $H^+$ is upper Hessenberg, restricting to columns 1 through $r$ gives $AV_mQ(:,1:r)=V_mQ(:,1:r)H_r^++(h^+V_mQe_{r+1}+\beta_m(e_m^*Qe_r)v_{m+1})e_r^*$, the stated identity with residual vector $g$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The vector $V_mQe_{r+1}$ is orthogonal to the first $r$ columns of $V_mQ$, and [F1] makes $v_{m+1}$ orthogonal to the range of $V_m$; hence $g$ is orthogonal to the retained columns. If $g\ne0$, normalization gives the next Arnoldi residual direction with coefficient $\|g\|_2$; if $g=0$, step 3.2 says $A$ maps the retained range into itself. [F1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

id: alg-block-lobpcg-with-rank-loss-status
kind: algorithm
title: "Finite-budget block LOBPCG for a Hermitian-definite pencil with explicit rank-loss status"
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: numerical-optimization-dynamics-2026-10-16
dependency_level: 1
deps:
  - def-b-inner-product-and-dual-norm-for-definite-pencil
  - def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum
  - thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms
justified_by: []
proof_strategy: direct
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: not-applicable
verification:
  precheck: n/a
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Peter Arbenz, Lecture Notes on Solving Large Scale Eigenvalue Problems, §13.6"
      url: "https://people.inf.ethz.ch/arbenz/ewp/Lnotes/lsevp.pdf"
    - title: "Andrew Knyazev, Recent implementations, applications, and extensions of LOBPCG, §1"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1708.08354"
---

## Definition

Let $A=A^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $B=B^*>0$, and let
$T=T^*>0$ be a fixed preconditioning operator. Here $B>0$ and $T>0$ mean
$x^*Bx>0$ and $x^*Tx>0$ for every nonzero $x$. The $B$-inner product and
norm are those of [[def-b-inner-product-and-dual-norm-for-definite-pencil]].
Choose a block width $1\le q\le n$, a residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a finite
iteration budget $N_{\max}\ge0$, and an initial matrix $X_0$ with
$X_0^*BX_0=I_q$. The output is a block of Ritz pairs and one of
`converged`, `budget-exhausted`, `rank-loss`, or `invalid-initial-block`.

1. If $X_0$ does not have full column rank or does not satisfy
   $X_0^*BX_0=I_q$, return `invalid-initial-block`. Compute the Rayleigh-Ritz eigenpairs in
   $\operatorname{range}(X_0)$, sorted increasingly, and let $\Theta_0$ be the
   diagonal matrix of the $q$ Ritz values. Set the previous search block
   $D_0$ empty and initialize the iteration counter $k=0$.

2. At iteration $k$, form the original residual block
   $R_k=AX_k-BX_k\Theta_k$. If every column has Euclidean norm at most
   $\tau$, return `converged`. If $k=N_{\max}$, return
   `budget-exhausted` with $(\Theta_k,X_k)$.

3. Compute the preconditioned residual block $W_k=TR_k$ and set
   $Y_k=[X_k,W_k,D_k]$, omitting the empty block at $k=0$. Compute an exact
   rank-revealing $B$-QR with column pivoting as follows. Starting with no
   columns in $Q_k$, for each remaining column $y_j$ of $Y_k$ compute its
   residual $c_j=y_j-Q_k(Q_k^*By_j)$ and choose a column with largest
   $B$-norm $\|c_j\|_B$ (break ties by original column order). If the largest
   residual norm is zero, stop; otherwise append the normalized residual to
   $Q_k$ and remove that pivot column. Let $s_k$ be the number of columns
   appended and let $\Pi_k$ record the pivot order followed by the unused
   columns. If $s_k<q$, return `rank-loss` with the current Ritz pairs; no
   projected solve is attempted on that branch. Otherwise set
   $$S_k=Q_k^*BY_k\Pi_k(:,1:s_k).$$
   The pivot construction gives
   $$Y_k\Pi_k(:,1:s_k)=Q_kS_k,\qquad Q_k^*BQ_k=I_{s_k},$$
   and $S_k$ is invertible because its selected columns are independent.
   Dependent trial columns are discarded and their count is recorded as a
   rank-compression diagnostic.

4. The projected matrix $Q_k^*AQ_k$ is Hermitian, hence normal, so its
   orthonormal eigenbasis and real eigenvalues are supplied by
   [[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]. Solve
   $Q_k^*AQ_kZ_k=Z_k\Theta_{k+1}$ and choose its $q$ smallest eigenvalues. Set
   $C_k=\Pi_k(:,1:s_k)S_k^{-1}Z_k$; then $Y_kC_k=Q_kZ_k$. Partition
   $C_k=\begin{bmatrix}C_X\\C_W\\C_D\end{bmatrix}$, omitting the $C_D$
   block when $D_k$ is empty. The projected metric is positive definite
   because for nonzero $z$, $(Q_kz)^*B(Q_kz)=\|z\|_2^2>0$. Set
   $$X_{k+1}=X_kC_X+W_kC_W+D_kC_D,\qquad D_{k+1}=W_kC_W+D_kC_D,$$
   again omitting the empty-block term. Let $\Theta_{k+1}$ be the selected
   diagonal Ritz-value matrix and increment $k$.

5. Repeat from step 2. No convergence, rate, or accuracy is asserted when the
   budget or rank-loss branch is returned. The exact SPD conditions on $B$ and
   $T$ define the permitted metric and preconditioner; no particular
   incomplete-factorization procedure is assumed.

id: thm-finite-budget-restarted-and-block-procedures-return-a-status
kind: theorem
title: "Finite-budget restarted Arnoldi and block LOBPCG return a status under finite-return primitives"
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: numerical-optimization-dynamics-2026-10-16
dependency_level: 2
deps:

justified_by: []

provenance:

  proof: ai-altered
verification:

sources:
  references:
    - title: "Yousef Saad, Numerical Methods for Large Eigenvalue Problems, second edition, §7.3"
      url: "https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~saad/eig_book_2ndEd.pdf"
    - title: "Peter Arbenz, Lecture Notes on Solving Large Scale Eigenvalue Problems, §§11.7 and 13.6"
      url: "https://people.inf.ethz.ch/arbenz/ewp/Lnotes/lsevp.pdf"
---

## Statement

Consider any execution of [[alg-thick-and-implicitly-restarted-arnoldi-with-locking]]
or [[alg-block-lobpcg-with-rank-loss-status]] on inputs satisfying that
procedure's stated hypotheses. Assume every invoked target rule returns in
finite work either a valid requested block or `unavailable`, every invoked
shift rule returns in finite work either a shift list of the required length
or `unavailable`, and every projected eigensolve, finite-dimensional
arithmetic, orthogonalization, and rank computation returns its exact value
in finite work. Then the execution returns one of the statuses listed by its
procedure after finitely many operations. In particular, the Arnoldi
procedure performs at most $N_{\max}$ restarts and at most $N_{\max}+1$
Arnoldi cycles, and the LOBPCG procedure performs at most $N_{\max}$ updates.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A valid finite-dimensional input to either procedure, finite
budgets $N_{\max}$, and the finite-return condition in the statement.

[F1] [[alg-thick-and-implicitly-restarted-arnoldi-with-locking]]: each cycle
uses at most $m$ Arnoldi steps, each no-lock implicit restart uses $p=m-r$
shifts, locked implicit-mode restarts use the thick fallback, and the restart
counter starts at zero and increases once per restart. The procedure either
returns when the counter equals $N_{\max}$, reports a listed target/shift
status, or reaches an earlier status condition.

[F2] [[alg-block-lobpcg-with-rank-loss-status]]: the iteration counter starts
at $k=0$, and iteration $k$ tests $k=N_{\max}$ before an update.

[F3] [[alg-block-lobpcg-with-rank-loss-status]]: every completed projected
update increments $k$ once; the rank-revealing orthogonalization processes
only the finitely many trial-block columns.

[A1] Each invoked target rule returns a valid requested block or
`unavailable`, and each invoked shift rule returns the required shift list or
`unavailable`, all in finite work. Every projected eigensolve and other
finite-dimensional arithmetic, orthogonalization, or rank computation returns
its exact value in finite work; no other primitive failure status is assumed.

## Proof

1.1 For thick or implicit restarted Arnoldi, one cycle has at most $m$
Arnoldi steps. The thick restart processes finite matrices and blocks using
finite exact rank-revealing orthogonalization loops, and its block-Arnoldi
queue processes at most $m$ basis columns once each; an unavailable target
selection, a missing target rule, or a wrong-size or dependent target block
returns `rank-loss`. An implicit restart
with no locked pairs uses
exactly $p=m-r$ shifts and finite QR steps; an unavailable or wrong-length
shift list returns `shift-count-unavailable`. The implicit-mode thick fallback
with locked pairs uses the same finite target and orthogonalization steps.
Assumption [A1] makes all other invoked rules and projected eigensolves
finite-return. Thus each cycle either returns a listed status or reaches its
single restart-counter update. [given, F1, A1, algebra]

1.2 For block LOBPCG, every pass through steps 1--4 is finite: its trial block has finitely many columns, its $B$-orthogonalization processes at most those columns, and the projected eigensolve and finite-dimensional operations return in finite work by [A1]. A pass either returns a status or completes one update and increments $k$. [given, F2, F3, A1, algebra]

2.1 The counter begins at $0$ and increases by one before each further cycle. After at most $N_{\max}$ such increments, the next completed cycle reaches the test $c=N_{\max}$ and returns `budget-exhausted` unless an earlier acceptance or breakdown status has already returned. The number of cycles is therefore at most $N_{\max}+1$, so the Arnoldi execution terminates. [F1, step 1.1, induction]

3.1 Starting from $k=0$, no more than $N_{\max}$ updates can occur. After those updates the next pass tests $k=N_{\max}$ and returns `budget-exhausted`, unless convergence or rank loss already returned. Hence the block LOBPCG execution terminates after finitely many operations. [F2, F3, step 1.2, induction] ∎

## Statement

Let $A=A^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and $B=B^*>0$. Write the generalized
eigenvalues of $(A,B)$ in increasing order
$\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n$. For a subspace $S$ with a full-column-rank
$B$-orthonormal basis matrix $Q_S$, let
$\theta_1(S)\le\cdots\le\theta_{\dim S}(S)$ be the eigenvalues of
$Q_S^*AQ_S$. These values are independent of the chosen $B$-orthonormal basis.
Then, for $1\le j\le\dim S$,
$$\lambda_j\le\theta_j(S).$$
If $S\subseteq T$ and $j\le\dim S$, then
$$\theta_j(T)\le\theta_j(S).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Hermitian matrix $A$, a Hermitian positive-definite matrix $B$,
and full-column-rank $B$-orthonormal basis matrices for the stated subspaces.

[F1] [[def-b-inner-product-and-dual-norm-for-definite-pencil]]: $\langle x,y\rangle_B=y^*Bx$ and $\|x\|_B^2=x^*Bx$.

[F2] [[thm-hermitian-definite-pencil-has-real-spectrum-and-b-orthogonal-eigenbasis]]: a Hermitian-definite pair $(A,B)$ has real generalized eigenvalues and a $B$-orthonormal eigenbasis.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $Q_S$, the compression $H_S=Q_S^*AQ_S$ is Hermitian. Diagonalize it with an orthonormal eigenbasis $z_1,\ldots,z_s$ and ordered eigenvalues $\theta_1(S)\le\cdots\le\theta_s(S)$; the vectors $Q_Sz_i$ are B-orthonormal and every Rayleigh quotient on $S$ is their weighted average. Any j-dimensional $W\subseteq S$ intersects $\operatorname{span}(Q_Sz_j,\ldots,Q_Sz_s)$ nontrivially by dimension count, so its maximum quotient is at least $\theta_j(S)$; equality is attained on $\operatorname{span}(Q_Sz_1,\ldots,Q_Sz_j)$. This proves the min-max formula, and a unitary change between B-orthonormal bases conjugates the compression, proving basis invariance. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Let $u_1,\ldots,u_n$ be the ambient B-orthonormal generalized eigenbasis from [F2], ordered by $\lambda_i$. Any j-dimensional $W\subseteq S$ intersects $\operatorname{span}(u_j,\ldots,u_n)$ nontrivially, again by dimension count. The quotient of a nonzero vector in that span is a weighted average of $\lambda_j,\ldots,\lambda_n$ and is at least $\lambda_j$; the min-max formula from step 1.1 gives $\theta_j(S)\ge\lambda_j$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $S\subseteq T$, every j-dimensional subspace considered for $\theta_j(S)$ is also available for $\theta_j(T)$. The minimum over the larger family therefore cannot be greater, so $\theta_j(T)\le\theta_j(S)$. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A=A^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $B=B^*>0$, and
$\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n$ be the generalized eigenvalues of $(A,B)$.
Fix $1\le q<n$ with the strict gap $\lambda_q<\lambda_{q+1}$ and let
$U=\operatorname{span}\{u_1,\ldots,u_q\}$ be the corresponding sum of the
first $q$ eigenspaces, with $(u_i)$ $B$-orthonormal. For a $q$-dimensional
trial subspace $S$ with $B$-orthonormal basis $Q$, define
$$P_Ux=\sum_{i=1}^q u_i(u_i^*Bx),\qquad \sin\vartheta=\sup_{\substack{x\in S\\\|x\|_B=1}}\|(I-P_U)x\|_B.$$
Let $\theta_1(S)\le\cdots\le\theta_q(S)$ be the generalized Ritz values
from [[lem-generalized-ritz-values-monotone-under-nested-subspaces]]. Then
$$\lambda_j\le\theta_j(S)\quad(1\le j\le q),\qquad \theta_q(S)\le\lambda_q+(\lambda_n-\lambda_q)\sin^2\vartheta.$$
The strict gap identifies $U$ uniquely; the estimate is a subspace enclosure,
not an iteration convergence rate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Hermitian-definite pair $(A,B)$, its ordered generalized
eigenvalues and $B$-orthonormal eigenbasis, the strict gap at $q$, and a
$q$-dimensional $B$-orthonormal trial basis $Q$ spanning $S$.

[F1] [[def-b-inner-product-and-dual-norm-for-definite-pencil]]: $\langle x,y\rangle_B=y^*Bx$ and $\|x\|_B^2=x^*Bx$.

[F2] [[thm-hermitian-definite-pencil-has-real-spectrum-and-b-orthogonal-eigenbasis]]: $A$ and $B$ have a $B$-orthonormal generalized eigenbasis with real eigenvalues.

[L1] [[lem-generalized-ritz-values-monotone-under-nested-subspaces]]: each selected Ritz value is at least the corresponding ambient generalized eigenvalue, and Ritz values decrease when the trial subspace is enlarged.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F2], write a B-unit vector $x\in S$ as $x=u+e$ with $u=P_Ux\in U$ and $e=(I-P_U)x\in U^{\perp_B}$. In the B-orthonormal generalized eigenbasis, if $x=\sum_i a_i u_i$, then $x^*Bx=\sum_i|a_i|^2$ and $x^*Ax=\sum_i\lambda_i|a_i|^2$. Thus $u^*Au\le\lambda_q u^*Bu$ and $e^*Ae\le\lambda_n e^*Be$; the cross terms vanish since $u_i^*Au_j=\lambda_j u_i^*Bu_j=0$ for $i\le q<j$. Therefore $x^*Ax/x^*Bx\le\lambda_q\|u\|_B^2+\lambda_n\|e\|_B^2=\lambda_q+(\lambda_n-\lambda_q)\|e\|_B^2$, which is at most the stated angle bound. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Diagonalizing the finite Hermitian compression shows that $\theta_q(S)$ is the maximum Rayleigh quotient on $S$, so step 1.1 gives its upper bound. The lower bounds $\lambda_j\le\theta_j(S)$ are [L1]. The strict gap isolates the first q eigenspaces, so their sum is unique; no step asserts an iteration rate. [given, F2, L1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, choose a shift
$\sigma\in\mathbb C$, and put $M=A-\sigma I$. This procedure returns candidate
values and their residual data; it asserts no convergence or forward-error
bound. Its branch statuses are `available`, `arnoldi-breakdown`,
`linear-solve-unavailable`, `zero-transformed-Ritz-value`,
`infinite-harmonic-value`, `projected-pencil-unresolved`,
`qz-budget-exhausted`, and `qz-certificate-inconclusive`.

**Shift-invert branch.** This branch requires $M$ to be invertible, equivalently
that $\sigma$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$ by
[[prop-eigenvalue-iff-shift-is-not-invertible]]. Its inputs also include a
nonzero starting vector $v$, an integer Arnoldi dimension $1\le m\le n$, a
residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and a solve routine. Normalize
$v_1=v/\|v\|_2$. For $j=1,\ldots,m$, request either the exact solution
$y_j=M^{-1}v_j$ or a computed vector $y_j$ together with its actual equation
residual $s_j=My_j-v_j$. If a requested solve is unavailable, return
`linear-solve-unavailable` with the residuals already recorded. Set $w=y_j$.
For $i=1,\ldots,j$, compute $h_{ij}=\langle w,v_i\rangle$ and replace
$w\gets w-h_{ij}v_i$. Repeat this pass once, adding each second-pass
coefficient to the corresponding $h_{ij}$. Set $h_{j+1,j}=\|w\|_2$. If this
norm is zero, set the current dimension to $k=j$ and stop with status
`arnoldi-breakdown`; otherwise set $v_{j+1}=w/h_{j+1,j}$. After $m$ columns,
set $k=m$ and stop with status `available`.
When every solve is exact, this is Arnoldi applied to $M^{-1}$. When any solve
is inexact, the projected matrix is only the one produced from the computed
vectors; the procedure makes no exact-Arnoldi or convergence claim for that
branch.

Compute the Ritz pairs $(\theta,z)$ of the current $k\times k$ matrix $H$ as
in [[def-ritz-values-and-ritz-vectors-from-arnoldi]], normalize $z$ to unit
norm, and lift $u=V_kz$. For each $\theta\ne0$, report the transformed candidate
$\lambda=\sigma+1/\theta$, the lifted vector $u$, and the directly computed
original residual $r_A=Au-\lambda u$. Mark this candidate accepted exactly
when $\|r_A\|_2\le\tau$. If $\theta=0$, assign no finite inverse map and mark
that candidate `zero-transformed-Ritz-value`. To record the solve-error
transfer for a candidate with $\theta\ne0$, request one additional solve
$My=u$; if it is available, store $s_0=My-u$ and $r_T=y-\theta u$ alongside
the directly computed residual $r_A$.
If this additional solve is unavailable, return
`linear-solve-unavailable` with the candidate and accumulated ledger.

**Harmonic Ritz branch.** This branch takes a full-column-rank trial basis
$U\in\mathbb C^{n\times k}$, $k\ge1$; it does not require $M$ to be
invertible. Form $W=MU$ and
$$G=W^*W=U^*M^*MU,\qquad C=W^*U=U^*M^*U.$$
Compute an exact column-pivoted QR of $W$ as in
[[def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations]] and let
$r_W$ be its exact rank. If $r_W<k$, choose $z\ne0$ with $Wz=0$. Then
$z^*G=(Wz)^*W=0$ and $z^*C=(Wz)^*U=0$. Thus the nonzero row
$z^*$ annihilates $G-\eta C$ for every $\eta$; if this matrix were invertible,
right multiplication by its inverse would force $z^*=0$, a contradiction.
Hence $G-\eta C$ is singular for every $\eta$; return
`projected-pencil-unresolved`. If $W$ has full column rank, then
$z^*Gz=\|Wz\|_2^2>0$ for every $z\ne0$. Thus $G$ is positive definite and
the pencil $G-\eta C$ is regular in the convention of
[[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]], since
$\det(G-0C)=\det G\ne0$.

Supply a finite QZ sweep budget $N\ge0$ and tolerance $\tau_{QZ}\ge0$, and run
[[alg-finite-budget-qz-iteration-with-deflation-and-residual]] on $(G,C)$.
Compute $G,C$ exactly in the mathematical procedure; a finite implementation
must include their formation errors in the perturbation ledger or return
`qz-certificate-inconclusive`. On `qz-computed`, require its exact-factor and
local-update certificates;
[[prop-finite-budget-qz-iteration-terminates-and-preserves-pencil-equivalence]]
then records equivalence to a perturbed projected pencil. For each diagonal
index $i$, set $\alpha_i=S_{ii}$ and $\beta_i=T_{ii}$. If
$(\alpha_i,\beta_i)=(0,0)$, return `projected-pencil-unresolved`; if
$\beta_i\ne0$, report the computed harmonic Ritz value
$\lambda_i=\sigma+\alpha_i/\beta_i$; if $\beta_i=0$, mark that candidate
`infinite-harmonic-value`. These are values of the computed perturbed
pencil, with the QZ residual and perturbation ledger retained; no exact-root,
eigenvector, or forward-error claim is made. Map a QZ `budget-exhausted` status
to `qz-budget-exhausted`; map a QZ `certificate-inconclusive` or `range-failure`
to `qz-certificate-inconclusive`; map `singular-pencil-suspected` to
`projected-pencil-unresolved`.

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $\sigma\in\mathbb C$, and
$M=A-\sigma I$ be invertible. Then a nonzero vector $u$ is an eigenvector of
$A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ if and only if it is an eigenvector of
$M^{-1}$ with eigenvalue $\theta=(\lambda-\sigma)^{-1}$. In particular,
$\lambda=\sigma+1/\theta$ and $\theta\ne0$.

For any nonzero candidate $u$, any $\theta\ne0$, and any computed vector $y$
with solve residual $s_0=My-u$, define the transformed residual
$r_T=y-\theta u$ and $\lambda=\sigma+1/\theta$. Then
$$ (A-\lambda I)u=\theta^{-1}(s_0-Mr_T), $$
and consequently
$$\|(A-\lambda I)u\|_2\le\frac{\|s_0\|_2+\|Mr_T\|_2}{|\theta|}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $M=A-\sigma I$ invertible, a nonzero vector $u$, a nonzero scalar
$\theta$, and a computed solve vector $y$ with $s_0=My-u$.

[F1] [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]: $Au=\lambda u$ with $u\ne0$ is the definition of an eigenpair.

[F2] [[alg-shift-invert-and-harmonic-ritz-extraction]]: the inexact candidate solve records $s_0=My-u$ and $r_T=y-\theta u$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $Au=\lambda u$, then $Mu=(\lambda-\sigma)u$. Invertibility of $M$ and $u\ne0$ imply $\lambda\ne\sigma$, so applying $M^{-1}$ gives $M^{-1}u=(\lambda-\sigma)^{-1}u$. Conversely, if $M^{-1}u=\theta u$ with $u\ne0$, multiplying by $M$ gives $Mu=\theta^{-1}u$; hence $Au=(\sigma+\theta^{-1})u$. Thus the eigenvalue map is exact and the inverse Ritz value cannot be zero. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 From [F2], $Mr_T=My-\theta Mu=u+s_0-\theta Mu$. Rearranging yields $Mu-\theta^{-1}u=\theta^{-1}(s_0-Mr_T)$. Since $M=A-\sigma I$ and $\lambda=\sigma+1/\theta$, the left side is $(A-\lambda I)u$, proving the residual identity. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Taking Euclidean norms in step 1.2 and applying the triangle inequality gives the stated residual bound, which keeps the solve residual $s_0$ and the transformed residual after multiplication by $M$ as separate terms. [step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $b$ be a
nonzero vector of matching size, and let $m\ge1$. Assume the Arnoldi process
for $(A,b)$ runs through step $m$ without breakdown. Let

$$Q_m=[v_1\,\dots\,v_m], \qquad Q_{m+1}=[v_1\,\dots\,v_{m+1}],$$

and let $\bar H_m=(h_{ij})_{1\le i\le m+1,\,1\le j\le m}$, where the Arnoldi
coefficients occupy the positions $i\le j+1$ and $h_{ij}:=0$ for $i>j+1$.
Then:

1. $v_1,\dots,v_m$ are orthonormal;
2. $\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\dots,v_m\}=K_m(A,b)$;
3. $\bar H_m$ has the rectangular upper-Hessenberg zero pattern
   $h_{ij}=0$ for $i>j+1$;
4. $AQ_m=Q_{m+1}\bar H_m$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A square matrix $A$ over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, a nonzero start vector $b$ of matching size, an integer $m\ge1$, and an Arnoldi run through step $m$ with no breakdown.

[F1] In Arnoldi, each step defines $w_j=Av_j-\sum_{i=1}^j h_{ij}v_i$ with $h_{ij}=\langle Av_j,v_i\rangle$, and when $h_{j+1,j}=\|w_j\|\ne0$ one sets $v_{j+1}=w_j/h_{j+1,j}$ ([[def-arnoldi-process]]).

[F2] For $m\ge1$, one has $K_m(A,b)=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\ldots,A^{m-1}b\}$ ([[def-krylov-subspace-of-a-matrix-and-start-vector]]).

[F3] The square-matrix upper-Hessenberg condition is the zero pattern $h_{ij}=0$ for $i>j+1$ ([[def-upper-hessenberg-and-real-symmetric-tridiagonal-matrices]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By construction in [F1], the vector $w_j$ is orthogonal to each $v_i$ for $1\le i\le j$, because $h_{ij}=\langle Av_j,v_i\rangle$ subtracts exactly the orthogonal projection of $Av_j$ onto $v_i$. Since there is no breakdown, $w_j\ne0$, so $v_{j+1}=w_j/\|w_j\|$ is a unit vector orthogonal to $v_1,\dots,v_j$. Starting from the unit vector $v_1=b/\|b\|$, induction gives orthonormality of $v_1,\dots,v_m$. [F1, algebra]

1.2 Again by [F1], each $v_{j+1}$ is a linear combination of $Av_j,v_1,\dots,v_j$. Induction using [F2] therefore gives $v_i\in K_i(A,b)\subseteq K_m(A,b)$ for $i\le m$. Conversely, $Av_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j+1} h_{ij}v_i$ lies in $\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\dots,v_{j+1}\}$, and induction from $v_1=b/\|b\|$ shows that $b,Ab,\dots,A^{m-1}b$ all lie in $\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\dots,v_m\}$. By [F2], the two spans are equal. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For each column $j$, the Arnoldi relation from [F1] involves only $v_1,\dots,v_{j+1}$. By the definition of $\bar H_m$ in the Statement, its remaining entries satisfy $h_{ij}=0$ for $i>j+1$, the same zero pattern as the square upper-Hessenberg condition [F3]. The column relations assemble exactly into $AQ_m=Q_{m+1}\bar H_m$. [F1, F3, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $A_0\in M_n(\mathbb F)$.

1. The **unshifted QR iteration** factors
   $$A_k=Q_kR_k$$
   with $Q_k$ unitary and $R_k$ upper triangular, then sets
   $$A_{k+1}:=R_kQ_k.$$
2. Given shifts $\mu_k\in\mathbb F$, the **shifted QR iteration** factors
   $$A_k-\mu_k I=Q_kR_k$$
   and sets
   $$A_{k+1}:=R_kQ_k+\mu_k I.$$
3. Given a declared tolerance $\tau_k\ge0$, **numerical deflation** at index
   $j$ occurs when $|(A_k)_{j+1,j}|\le\tau_k$: that entry is then replaced by
   $0$, splitting the matrix into the two diagonal blocks separated at index
   $j$. **Exact deflation** is the special case $\tau_k=0$.
4. For a real symmetric tridiagonal matrix, the **Wilkinson shift** is the
   eigenvalue of the trailing $2\times2$ principal block that is nearer to the
   bottom-right entry; away from a tie, this eigenvalue is unique.

## Statement

If $H$ is upper Hessenberg and a shifted QR step factors
$H-\mu I=QR$ using the standard adjacent-row Givens eliminations, then

$$ H_+:=RQ+\mu I $$

is again upper Hessenberg.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An upper Hessenberg matrix $H$ and a shifted QR factorisation $H-\mu I=QR$ built from adjacent Givens eliminations.

[L1] A shifted QR step is $H_+=RQ+\mu I$ ([[def-unshifted-and-shifted-qr-iteration-with-deflation-and-wilkinson-shift]]).

[L2] Upper Hessenberg means all entries below the first subdiagonal vanish ([[def-upper-hessenberg-and-real-symmetric-tridiagonal-matrices]]).

[L3] Givens transformations are unitary and annihilate a chosen adjacent entry ([[def-real-and-complex-givens-transformations]], [[thm-householder-reflectors-and-givens-transformations-are-unitary-and-annihilate-targeted-entries]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Because $H-\mu I$ is upper Hessenberg, each subdiagonal entry can be annihilated by an adjacent Givens rotation acting only on two consecutive rows. By [L3], the product of these rotations gives $Q$ and an upper triangular $R$. [L2, L3, construct]

2.1 Right-multiplying an upper triangular matrix by one adjacent Givens rotation can create a nonzero entry only one row below the diagonal in the two affected columns. Repeating this through the same adjacent sequence keeps $RQ$ upper Hessenberg. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Adding $\mu I$ changes only diagonal entries, so [L1] and step 2.1 show that $H_+=RQ+\mu I$ is again upper Hessenberg. [L1, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

A square matrix $H=(h_{ij})$ is **upper Hessenberg** when
$h_{ij}=0$ for every $i>j+1$, so entries below the first subdiagonal vanish.

A real symmetric matrix $T=(t_{ij})$ is **tridiagonal** when
$t_{ij}=0$ for every $|i-j|>1$. Thus a real symmetric tridiagonal matrix is
exactly a symmetric upper Hessenberg matrix.

## Definition

Let $n\ge 2$ and let $0\le i<j\le n-1$.

A **real Givens rotation** in the $(i,j)$-plane is the identity matrix except on
rows and columns $i,j$, where it has the $2\times 2$ block

$$\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-s&c\end{pmatrix}\qquad(c,s\in\mathbb R,\ c^2+s^2=1).$$A **complex Givens transformation** in the $(i,j)$-plane is the identity except on rows and columns $i,j$, where it has block$$\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix},$$

with $c\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}$, $s\in\mathbb C$, and $c^2+|s|^2=1$. The modulus
$|s|$ is the one from [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]].

Such transformations act only on the two chosen coordinates and are designed to
zero one targeted entry while preserving the Euclidean norm from
[[def-inner-product-norm]].

## Definition

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ with $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
and $m\ge n$.

A **full QR factorisation** of $A$ is a factorisation

$$A=QR,$$where $Q\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ is orthogonal or unitary and $R\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ is upper trapezoidal. A **reduced QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A=\widehat Q\widehat R,$$where $\widehat Q\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ has orthonormal columns ($\widehat Q^*\widehat Q=I_n$) and $\widehat R\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ is upper triangular. A **column-pivoted QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A\Pi=\widehat Q R,$$

where $\Pi$ is a permutation matrix acting on columns, $\widehat Q$ has
orthonormal columns, and $R$ is upper trapezoidal or upper triangular according
to whether the full or reduced form is used. Computationally, one obtains these
factorisations by successive Householder reflectors or Givens transformations
that zero entries below the diagonal, with the pivoted version choosing the next
column after a permutation.

## Definition

Let $B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
be Hermitian positive definite, with Cholesky factor $B=LL^*$ and $L$ lower
triangular with positive diagonal. This factor exists and is unique by
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Define the linear-first **B-inner product** by
$$\langle x,y\rangle_B:=y^*Bx,$$
the **B-norm** by
$$\|x\|_B:=\|L^*x\|_2=\sqrt{x^*Bx},$$
and the **B-dual residual norm** by
$$\|r\|_{B^{-1}}:=\|L^{-1}r\|_2 =\sqrt{r^*B^{-1}r}.$$
The B-orthogonality condition is $x^*By=0$; since $B=B^*$ it is equivalent
to $\langle x,y\rangle_B=0$.

## Statement

Let $A=A^*$ and let $B=B^*$ be positive definite in
$\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, where $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
If $B=LL^*$ is its Cholesky factorisation, then
$$C=L^{-1}AL^{-*}$$
is self-adjoint and has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$. The vectors
$$x_i=L^{-*}y_i\quad (i=1,\ldots,n)$$
form a basis satisfying $Ax_i=\lambda_iBx_i$ and
$x_i^*Bx_j=\delta_{ij}$. The generalized eigenvalues of $(A,B)$ are exactly
$[\lambda_i:1]$; none is infinite.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real symmetric or complex Hermitian matrix $A$ and a Hermitian
positive-definite matrix $B$ of the same positive order.

[F1] [[def-b-inner-product-and-dual-norm-for-definite-pencil]]: for the unique
Cholesky factor $B=LL^*$, $\|x\|_B=\|L^*x\|_2$, and B-orthonormality means
$x_i^*Bx_j=\delta_{ij}$.

[F2] [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]:
$B=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and positive diagonal, and $L$ is unique.

[F3] [[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]: the determinant of a
triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.

[F4] [[thm-operator-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]: a finite-dimensional
operator over a field is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.

[F5] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]: a real
self-adjoint endomorphism has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F6] [[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]: a complex
normal endomorphism has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F7] [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]: determinants multiply under matrix
products.

[F8] [[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]]: homogeneous roots of
$\det(\beta A-\alpha B)$ are the generalized eigenvalues.

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], $L$ is lower triangular with positive diagonal. [F3] gives $\det L\ne0$, and [F4] therefore makes $L$ invertible. Hence $C=L^{-1}AL^{-*}$ is defined. Taking adjoints and using $A=A^*$ gives $C^*=L^{-1}AL^{-*}=C$. [given, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Regard $C$ as a real or complex endomorphism with the Euclidean inner product. In the real case [F5] applies; in the complex case $C=C^*$ implies $C$ is normal, so [F6] applies. Thus there are orthonormal $y_i$ and real $\lambda_i$ with $Cy_i=\lambda_i y_i$. [step 1.1, F5, F6, algebra]

3.1 Set $x_i=L^{-*}y_i$. Then $Ax_i=AL^{-*}y_i=L Cy_i=\lambda_iLy_i=\lambda_iBx_i,$ and $x_i^*Bx_j=y_i^*L^{-1}LL^*L^{-*}y_j=y_i^*y_j=\delta_{ij}.$ The invertible change of variables $L^{-*}$ sends the basis $(y_i)$ to a basis $(x_i)$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

4.1 For every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$, $A-\lambda B=L(C-\lambda I)L^*$, so $\det(A-\lambda B)=\det(L)\det(C-\lambda I)\det(L^*).$ The diagonalisation from step 2.1 expresses $C=UDU^*$ with $D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$ and $U$ unitary. By [F7], $\det(C-\lambda I)=\det(U)\det(D-\lambda I)\det(U^*)$ and $\det(U)\det(U^*)=\det(UU^*)=\det I=1$. Applying [F3] to the diagonal matrix gives $\det(C-\lambda I)=\prod_i(\lambda_i-\lambda)$. Also $\det(L)$ and $\det(L^*)$ are nonzero by step 1.1, so the finite roots of $\det(A-\lambda B)$ are exactly the real $\lambda_i$. Finally $\det(B)=\det(L)\det(L^*)\ne0$, so $[1:0]$ is not a homogeneous root. [F2, F3, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

## Definition

Input a regular pencil $(A,B)$ with $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$,
$n\ge1$, a nonnegative integer sweep budget $N$, and a finite stored real tolerance
$\tau\ge0$. Real input data are embedded in $\mathbb C$. Scalar updates of the
stored matrices use the operationwise model of
[[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]].
Use the canonical stored Givens generator and application order of
[[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]], with the common-pair
orientations and explicit coefficients $v,h,\eta$ of
[[lem-qz-two-sided-local-computed-update-bound]]. Generate each rotation ONCE
and apply its same stored coefficients to BOTH matrices. Retain the exact
normalized unitary representatives as product records, never as purported
stored dense unitary matrices. Left rotations annihilate a column's second
entry; right rotations annihilating a row's first entry use the coordinate
reversal/adjoint construction of that lemma. After each genuine matrix target
application write only its intended target to exact zero and include that
write in the local coefficient $\eta$. An external-vector application has
coefficient $v$ and no matrix-target overwrite. Local roundoff certification
requires $0<u<1$; otherwise retain diagnostics with `certificate-inconclusive`. Record each elementary
rotation separately. If the source cannot produce its admissible factor,
return `range-failure` or `certificate-inconclusive` with diagnostics.

1. Execute the finite index loops of
[[alg-generalized-hessenberg-triangular-reduction]] with these COMPUTED common
rotations: triangularize $B$ with left targets $B_{i,j}$; then reduce $A$ with
left targets $A_{i,j}$ followed by right targets $B_{i,i-1}$. Every application
updates both whole arrays. The exact initializer and
[[prop-generalized-hessenberg-triangular-reduction-preserves-form-and-equivalence]]
supply the index schedule and support induction, not exact rounded
reconstruction. Retain each local factor and residual defined against its
exact representative. Include structural target writes in that local
arithmetic residual. Record all OTHER explicit zero writes separately: their
post-action perturbations are pulled back by the local factor adjoints before
entering the pre-action $D_j^A,D_j^B$ ledger. A pure tolerance write is an
identity-factor stage. Never count a structural write twice.

Initialize the sweep counter to zero. Process active blocks in increasing first
index, splitting them at exact zero subdiagonals of $H$. In each deflation
pass execute step 2, then repeat step 3 for the smallest available non-isolated
zero diagonal of $T$ until none remains or a status exits. Test step 5 before
starting a sweep: if the target is absent and the counter equals $N$, return
`budget-exhausted`. Otherwise increment the counter, execute step 4 on all
remaining active blocks, and repeat the deflation pass. In particular $N=0$
permits initialization/deflation but no step-4 sweep.

2. On each active block $H_{a:b,a:b},T_{a:b,a:b}$, apply the following deflation
tests before a sweep. For $i=a,\ldots,b-1$, set $H_{i+1,i}$ to zero when
$$|H_{i+1,i}|\le\tau\bigl(|H_{i,i}|+|H_{i+1,i+1}|\bigr),$$
and record its old value in $D^A$. For $k=a,\ldots,b$, set $T_{k,k}$ to zero when
$$|T_{k,k}|\le\tau\bigl(|T_{k-1,k}|+|T_{k,k+1}|\bigr),$$
using zero for a missing boundary term, and record the old value in $D^B$.
Evaluate each displayed modulus by the canonical rounded scaled two-component
norm; evaluate its additions and tolerance product with the declared rounded
real operations, then compare the stored finite values exactly. Excluded
operations return `range-failure`. The tests mean these rounded comparisons,
not an assertion about exact moduli at the threshold. Save the actual old
entries, so their deflation perturbations remain exact regardless of the test.
A one-by-one diagonal pair at $k$ is isolated when $H_{k,k-1}=0$ and
$H_{k+1,k}=0$, omitting a boundary entry when $k=a$ or $k=b$. If it has
$T_{k,k}=0$ and $H_{k,k}\ne0$, report an infinite candidate for the computed pencil and deflate it
from the active block. If the isolated diagonal pair is $(0,0)$, return
`singular-pencil-suspected` without assigning an eigenvalue.

3. To move a non-isolated zero $T_{k,k}$ to the top of its active block, for
$j=k-1,k-2,\ldots,a$ apply a right Givens factor on columns $j,j+1$ that
zeros $T_{j,j}$, then, when $j+2\le b$, a left Givens factor on rows
$j+1,j+2$ that zeros the resulting bulge $H_{j+2,j}$. Finally, when $a<b$,
apply a left Givens factor on rows $a,a+1$ to zero $H_{a+1,a}$. Record all rounded update residuals and target writes. If this isolates $(H_{a,a},T_{a,a})=(h,0)$ with $h\ne0$, report
the infinite candidate and remove the first row/column from the active block.
If the isolated pair is $(0,0)$, return `singular-pencil-suspected`; if isolation
fails, return `certificate-inconclusive`. Each successful isolation removes
one index, so at most $n$ such removals occur.

4. For each remaining active block with more than one row in the current
sweep, choose the homogeneous shift $[\alpha:\beta]=[H_{b,b}:T_{b,b}]$ if this pair is nonzero and
$T_{b,b}\ne0$; if $T_{b,b}=0$, use $[0:1]$. Form
$$x=(\beta H_{a:b,a:b}-\alpha T_{a:b,a:b})e_1.$$
Compute the first two components of $x$ using the declared rounded complex
products/subtractions and generate a left Givens factor from that stored
external vector. Apply it to both matrices without a matrix-target overwrite.
Its rounding changes the selected factor, not its application certificate. Apply a right Givens factor to columns $1,2$ to restore triangularity
of $T$. For $j=2,\ldots,b-a$, alternate a left Givens factor on rows $j,j+1$
to zero the current Hessenberg bulge and a right Givens factor on columns
$j,j+1$ to zero the resulting subdiagonal entry of $T$. Update and retain the
products $Q,Z$; record every local residual including its structural target
write. Indices $1,2,j,j+1$ here are relative to the active block; apply the
embedded transformations to the entire pair, retaining the transformed off-block data. All divisions by a generalized eigenvalue ratio are avoided.

5. After each infinite isolation and before every successful return, scan all
isolated diagonal pairs. Any $(0,0)$ pair returns `singular-pencil-suspected`
without an eigenvalue. Stop with `qz-computed` only when $H$ is upper triangular
and every diagonal pair is nonzero. Otherwise stop after $N$ sweeps with
`budget-exhausted`. Range failures return `range-failure` with partial factors;
unavailable local certificates return `certificate-inconclusive`. Neither a
rounded diagnostic nor a tolerance-induced infinite candidate asserts an exact
infinite eigenvalue of the original pencil.

For local-accumulation bounds use $\ell_j=\eta$ for matrix-target actions and
$\ell_j=v$ for external-vector/raw actions, plus the separately saved actual
tolerance perturbations. For an independent residual certificate execute the
factor-action/column procedure of
[[lem-qz-two-sided-local-computed-update-bound]]: use stored raw kernels without
zero overwrites, propagate their $v$ allowances, use
[[lem-rounded-linear-and-normal-residual-certificates]] only on STORED matvec
inputs, and include the final subtraction allowance. Exact normalized factor
entries are not silently treated as stored inputs. Evaluate each certificate
using the finite exact real-controller expression trees/loops in the local
lemma and component absolute sums as norm upper bounds. Controller operations
are separate from rounded update arithmetic; for rational/binary stored data
and rational $u$ this is exact rational computation. No opaque certification
oracle is used. Failure of this residual route's dimension/range hypotheses
makes that route inconclusive and does not invalidate a valid independent
local-accumulation bound. Always retain available diagnostics.

The output is $(Q,S,T,Z,\text{status})$, the exact factor products when
available, the raw residuals $R_A=Q^*AZ-S$ and $R_B=Q^*BZ-T$, and the recorded
local arithmetic and deflation perturbations. The procedure asserts no
unconditional convergence or small-roundoff bound.

deflation perturbation pair. This proposition gives no bound on its size.

**Given:** The finite input, budget $N$, tolerance $\tau$, and operationwise
finite-arithmetic model stated in the algorithm.

[F1] [[alg-finite-budget-qz-iteration-with-deflation-and-residual]] has finite
loops, a finite sweep budget, explicit range-failure handling, and records each
arithmetic residual and each assigned structural zero.

[F2] [[prop-generalized-hessenberg-triangular-reduction-preserves-form-and-equivalence]]:
the exact initialization gives the finite index schedule and support induction; numerical reconstruction instead uses [F5].

[F3] [[thm-householder-reflectors-and-givens-transformations-are-unitary-and-annihilate-targeted-entries]]:

[F4] [[lem-two-sided-unitary-equivalence-errors-accumulate-for-pencil]]:
local left/right unitary updates with local arithmetic and deflation residuals

2.2 For a run with certified factors, each local update has the form $A_j=Q_j^*(A_{j-1}+E_j^A+D_j^A)Z_j$ and $B_j=Q_j^*(B_{j-1}+E_j^B+D_j^B)Z_j$, where $E_j$ includes the structural target write and $D_j$ is the saved separate tolerance write, pulled back from post-action coordinates as required by [F5]. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Before `qz-computed`, both arrays are triangular and all diagonal pairs are nonzero. Their homogeneous determinant is $\prod_k(\beta S_{kk}-\alpha T_{kk})$, a product of nonzero linear polynomials, hence is not identically zero. The returned pencil is regular; any label with second coordinate zero is an infinite candidate of this returned perturbed pencil. ## Definition

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$. Let mortality and fertility be bounded Lipschitz functions $\mu,\beta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, and let $n_0\in L^1(0,\infty)$ be nonnegative. The **linear age-structured renewal transport problem** is

$$n_t(t,a)+n_a(t,a)=-\mu(a)n(t,a),\qquad a>0,\quad 0<t\le T,$$

with initial density $n(0,a)=n_0(a)$ and inflow condition

$$n(t,0)=B(t),\qquad B(t):=\int_0^\infty \beta(a)n(t,a)\,da.$$

Here $a$ is age, $B$ is the birth rate, and the characteristic age path solves the first-order initial value problem $a'(s)=1$ in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], hence $a(s)=a(0)+s$. Define survival from age $a$ over duration $s\ge0$ by

$$S(a,s):=\exp\!\left(-\int_a^{a+s}\mu(r)\,dr\right).$$

A **weak solution** on $[0,T]$ is a nonnegative $n\in C([0,T];L^1(0,\infty))$ with continuous $B:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$ and, for every $\phi\in C_c^1([0,T]\times[0,\infty))$ with $\phi(T,a)=0$,

$$-\int_0^T\!\int_0^\infty n(t,a)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu(a)\phi)\,da\,dt=\int_0^\infty n_0(a)\phi(0,a)\,da+\int_0^T B(t)\phi(t,0)\,dt.$$

A **mild solution** is a weak solution that also satisfies, for almost every $a\ge0$,

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)S(a-t,t),&a\ge t,\\B(t-a)S(0,a),&0\le a<t,\end{cases}$$

The formula follows the age characteristics $a'(s)=1$ and their mortality survival. No delay equation or finite-age cutoff is identified with this model by definition.

## Definition

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a nondegenerate fixed size interval $[0,X]$ with $X>0$. Let $g,\mu,\gamma:[0,X]\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded Lipschitz functions, with $g(x)\ge g_{\min}>0$. Here $g$ is size growth, $\mu$ is ordinary mortality, and $\gamma$ is the rate at which a dividing parent is removed. For each parent size $y$, let $K_y$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure of daughter sizes, supported on $[0,y]$. Assume $y\mapsto K_y(E)$ is measurable for every Borel set $E\subseteq[0,X]$, and that the number moment $k_0(y):=K_y([0,y])$ is uniformly bounded; the size moment $k_1(y):=\int_{[0,y]}x\,K_y(dx)$ is then finite. The **size-structured transport and division model** is

$$\partial_t n+\partial_x(gn)=-(\mu+\gamma)n+\int_{[0,X]}K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy,\qquad 0<x<X,$$

with zero incoming flux at $x=0$ and absorbing outflow $g(X)n(t,X)$ at $x=X$. Let $\Pi_{[0,X]}(x):=\min\{X,\max\{0,x\}\}$ and extend the growth field to $\widetilde g(x):=g(\Pi_{[0,X]}(x))$ on $\mathbb R$. This is a bounded Lipschitz vector field. By [[thm-size-structured-positivity-number-and-weighted-moment-identities]], its IVP has a unique solution on the finite time horizon; a model characteristic is this solution restricted to the interval from its initial size until its first hitting of $X$, including that hitting time when it occurs by $T$. On this restricted interval, $\widetilde g=g$. The characteristic is understood as a first-order IVP solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. The weak equation is obtained by testing against $\phi\in C^1([0,X])$: transport contributes $\int_0^Xg\phi'n$, mortality and parent removal contribute $-\int_0^X(\mu+\gamma)\phi n$, division contributes $\int_0^X\int\phi(x)K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy$, and the upper boundary contributes $-\phi(X)g(X)n(t,X)$. The interval is fixed; moving boundaries, zero growth and discontinuous coefficients are outside this definition.

## Statement

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], put $M(a)=\int_0^a\mu(r)\,dr$, $K(a)=\beta(a)e^{-M(a)}$, and

$$G(t)=\int_0^\infty \beta(x+t)\exp\!\left(-\int_x^{x+t}\mu(r)\,dr\right)n_0(x)\,dx.$$

There is a unique mild solution. Its birth rate is the unique continuous solution of

$$B(t)=G(t)+\int_0^t K(a)B(t-a)\,da,$$

and its density, for almost every $a\ge0$, is

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)\exp\!\left(-\int_{a-t}^{a}\mu(r)\,dr\right),&a\ge t,\\ B(t-a)e^{-M(a)},&0\le a<t.\end{cases}$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The model [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]] with bounded nonnegative Lipschitz $\mu,\beta$ and $n_0\in L^1_+$.

[F1] [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]]: characteristic age paths solve $a'=1$, survival is $S(a,s)=\exp(-\int_a^{a+s}\mu)$, and a mild solution satisfies the renewal boundary equation.

[F2] [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]: a solution of a first-order initial value problem is differentiable along its interval and satisfies its differential equation and initial value.

## Proof

1.1 The characteristic path through age $x$ at time $0$ is $a(s)=x+s$ by [F1] and [F2]. Along it the PDE gives $\frac{d}{ds}n(s,x+s)=-\mu(x+s)n(s,x+s)$, so integrating the scalar equation yields $n(t,x+t)=n_0(x)\exp(-\int_x^{x+t}\mu)$. A characteristic entering at age $0$ at time $t-a$ instead starts with value $B(t-a)$ and is multiplied by $e^{-M(a)}$, giving the two branches in the Statement. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Substitute the two branches into $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$ and split at $a=t$. In the old-cohort part set $x=a-t$; the result is exactly $G(t)+\int_0^t\beta(a)e^{-M(a)}B(t-a)\,da$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 The functions $K$ and $G$ are continuous. Indeed, $K$ is a product of Lipschitz functions; for $s,t\in[0,T]$, the integrand multiplier in $G$ changes by at most $(\operatorname{Lip}(\beta)+\|\beta\|_\infty\|\mu\|_\infty)|t-s|$, since $|e^{-u}-e^{-v}|\le|u-v|$ for $u,v\ge0$. Multiplication by $n_0\in L^1$ and integration gives continuity of $G$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.2 On any interval of length $\tau$ with $\tau\|K\|_\infty<1$, the right side of the Volterra equation is a contraction in the sup norm on continuous birth-rate functions: the difference of two outputs is bounded by $\tau\|K\|_\infty$ times the input difference. If $\|K\|_\infty=0$, the equation is simply $B=G$. Starting at time zero and then treating the already determined history as a fixed forcing term, finitely many such intervals cover $[0,T]$; each interval therefore has one continuous solution and the solutions agree at their shared endpoints. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 When $n_0\ge0$, $G,K\ge0$. Picard iteration from the zero function on the first interval preserves nonnegativity and converges to its unique fixed point; the same argument applies on each continuation interval because its known-history forcing is nonnegative. Thus $B\ge0$, and the characteristic formula gives $n\ge0$. [given, step 2.2, induction, algebra]

3.2 The formula has finite $L^1$ norm because its old-cohort contribution is at most $\|n_0\|_1$ and its newborn contribution is at most $\int_0^t B(s)\,ds$. On the old branch, continuity in time follows from translation continuity of $n_0$ in $L^1$ and dominated convergence for the survival multiplier. On the newborn branch, continuity follows from continuity and boundedness of $B$ and $S$, with the interval of newly entering cohorts having length tending to zero. Thus $n\in C([0,T];L^1)$. [given, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $\phi\in C_c^1([0,T]\times[0,\infty))$ satisfy $\phi(T,a)=0$. On an initial cohort with coordinate $x=a-t\ge0$, the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{dt}[n_0(x)S(x,t)\phi(t,x+t)]=n(t,x+t)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu\phi)(t,x+t)$ for almost every $t$. Integrating from $0$ to $T$ makes the terminal term zero and leaves $-n_0(x)\phi(0,x)$; integration over $x\ge0$ gives the initial-data contribution to the weak identity. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

4.2 For a newborn cohort with birth time $s=t-a\ge0$, the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{da}[B(s)S(0,a)\phi(s+a,a)]=n(s+a,a)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu\phi)(s+a,a)$. Integrating from $a=0$ to $T-s$ gives $-B(s)\phi(s,0)$ because $\phi(T,T-s)=0$; integrating over $s\in[0,T]$ gives the renewal-boundary contribution. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

4.3 The old-cohort region $a\ge t$ and newborn region $a<t$ partition the time-age domain up to a measure-zero diagonal. Adding their integrals from steps 4.1 and 4.2, then multiplying by $-1$, gives exactly the weak identity in [F1] with initial term $\int n_0(x)\phi(0,x)dx$ and boundary term $\int_0^T B(s)\phi(s,0)ds$. Step 1.2 gives $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)da$, and step 3.2 gives $n\in C([0,T];L^1)$ and nonnegativity. Thus the characteristic formula is a weak, hence mild, solution. [F1, step 1.2, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra]

5.1 Any mild solution has a birth rate satisfying the Volterra equation in step 1.2. Uniqueness from step 2.2 forces that same birth rate, and the characteristic formula in step 1.1 then forces the same density. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.2] ∎

## Definition

Input a partition $0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_J=X$ with $J\ge1$, a time step $\Delta t>0$, a nonnegative current mass vector $M^k=(M_j^k)_{j=1}^J$, and the coefficients and kernel from [[def-size-structured-transport-and-division-kernel]]. Partition $[0,X]$ into disjoint cells $C_j=[x_{j-1},x_j)$ for $j<J$ and $C_J=[x_{J-1},X]$, with widths $h_j=x_j-x_{j-1}>0$ and centers $x_j^c=(x_{j-1}+x_j)/2$. Set $u_j^k=M_j^k/h_j$, the incoming flux $F_0^k=0$, the internal and outgoing upwind fluxes $F_j^k=g(x_j)u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$, and $d_j=\mu(x_j^c)+\gamma(x_j^c)$.

For each parent cell $C_\ell$, form nonnegative daughter coefficients

$$A_{j\ell}=\frac{1}{h_\ell}\,Q_M\bigl(y\mapsto K_y(C_j);x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1\bigr),$$

using [[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]] on the parent-size interval. Since the one-panel midpoint rule is $Q_M(f;x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1)=h_\ell f(x_\ell^c)$, this gives $A_{j\ell}=K_{x_\ell^c}(C_j)\ge0$. If $\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)>1$ for any cell, return `invalid-cfl` without an update. Otherwise the finite-volume update is

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,d_jM_j^k+\Delta t\sum_{\ell=1}^JA_{j\ell}M_\ell^k.$$

The flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow. The admissible variable-width CFL is $\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)\le1$ for every cell. If a grid or any required coefficient/kernel evaluation fails, return failure without a partial update. Otherwise return $M^{k+1}$ together with the fluxes and daughter coefficients used in the step.

## Definition

Input a finite horizon $T>0$, a time step $\Delta t>0$, an age cutoff $A>0$, bounded nonnegative rates $\mu,\beta$ on $[0,A]$, and a finite positive initial quadrature $(a_i,m_i^0)_{i=1}^I$ supported in $[0,A)$ for the initial age measure on that interval. Set $N=\lfloor T/\Delta t\rfloor$; the procedure returns levels at $t_k=k\Delta t$ for $0\le k\le N$, with final time $N\Delta t\le T$. One option is the composite midpoint rule on a partition of $[0,A]$: for each panel midpoint $a_i$, set $m_i^0=\Delta a\,n_0(a_i)$. A cohort at age $a_i^k$ and mass $m_i^k$ follows the exact age characteristic

$$a_i^{k+1}=a_i^k+\Delta t$$

and updates its survival mass by forward Euler,

$$m_i^{k+1}=(1-\Delta t\,\mu(a_i^k))m_i^k.$$

If $\Delta t\|\mu\|_\infty>1$, return status invalid-step with no updates. Otherwise initialize the birth and outflow records as empty and set $\nu_h^0=\sum_i m_i^0\delta_{a_i^0}$. For each $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, first calculate $B_h^k=\sum_i\beta(a_i^k)m_i^k$. Advance every existing cohort by $a_i^{k+1}=a_i^k+\Delta t$ and update its survival mass by $m_i^{k+1}=(1-\Delta t\mu(a_i^k))m_i^k$. If an updated age is at least $A$, record that updated mass as discrete outflow and discard the cohort; otherwise retain it. Then insert a newborn cohort of age $0$ and mass $\Delta t B_h^k$ at time $t_{k+1}$. Record $B_h^k$ and the step's outflow, and form $\nu_h^{k+1}$ from the retained cohorts and this newborn. A failed rate evaluation returns failure with no partial update. The procedure returns the finite sequence $(\nu_h^k)_{k=0}^N$ and its birth/outflow records. The bounded-Lipschitz quadrature defect of the initial measure and the Euler survival error are separate inputs to any consistency claim.

## Definition

Fix $0<T<A$, bounded nonnegative Lipschitz rates $\mu,\beta:[0,A]\to[0,\infty)$, and initial density $n_0^A\in L^1_+(0,A)$. The **finite-age renewal model with absorbing outflow** is the age transport problem on $0<a<A$ with the same renewal inflow $B_A(t)=\int_0^A\beta(a)n^A(t,a)\,da$ as in [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]]. A cohort follows age speed $1$, retains its mortality survival $S(a,s)$ until it reaches $A$, and is then removed; no cohort enters from ages above $A$. The initial density is $n_0^A$ on $[0,A]$. A mild solution is the characteristic formula on $0<a<A$, with an initial-cohort branch for $a\ge t$, a newborn branch for $a<t$, and zero extension to $a\ge A$. Since $A>T$, no cohort born during $[0,T]$ reaches the outflow boundary.

## Statement

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], let $\beta_\infty=\|\beta\|_\infty$. The solution map $S_{\mu,\beta}(t):n_0\mapsto n(t,\cdot)$ is linear and positive, and

$$\|S_{\mu,\beta}(t)n_0\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty t}\|n_0\|_1.$$

If $n,\widetilde n$ use possibly different nonnegative bounded coefficients $(\mu,\beta)$ and $(\widetilde\mu,\widetilde\beta)$ and initial data $n_0,\widetilde n_0$, put $\delta=\|\mu-\widetilde\mu\|_\infty+\|\beta-\widetilde\beta\|_\infty$ and $\widetilde\beta_\infty=\|\widetilde\beta\|_\infty$. Then

$$\|n(t)-\widetilde n(t)\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty t}\left(\|n_0-\widetilde n_0\|_1+\delta t e^{\widetilde\beta_\infty t}\|\widetilde n_0\|_1\right).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two age-renewal models and the characteristic mild solutions supplied by [[thm-age-structured-renewal-characteristic-solution]].

[F1] [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]]: $\mu,\beta$ are nonnegative and bounded, the inflow is $B(t)=\int\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$, and survival is the exponential along an age characteristic.

[F2] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-characteristic-solution]]: each nonnegative initial density has one nonnegative mild solution, given by the characteristic formula and Volterra birth equation.

[F3] [[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]: if $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_0^t b(s)u(s)\,ds$ with nonnegative continuous $u,b$ and nondecreasing $a$, then $u(t)\le a(t)e^{\int_0^t b}$.

## Proof

1.1 The formula in [F2] is linear in $n_0$, and uniqueness in [F2] implies that the solution for a sum of two initial data is the sum of their solutions and that scalar multiples are preserved. Nonnegative $n_0$ gives nonnegative $G$, Volterra kernel and density by [F1]–[F2], so the solution operator is positive. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Integrating the two characteristic branches in [F2] gives $N(t)=\int_0^\infty n_0(x)S(x,t)\,dx+\int_0^t B(t-a)S(0,a)\,da$. Bounded $\mu$ and continuous $B$ permit differentiation under these integrals; using $\partial_tS(x,t)=-\mu(x+t)S(x,t)$ and $\partial_aS(0,a)=-\mu(a)S(0,a)$ yields $N'(t)=B(t)-\int_0^\infty\mu(a)n(t,a)\,da$ for almost every $t$. Since $0\le B(t)\le\beta_\infty N(t)$ and $\mu n\ge0$, we have $N'(t)\le\beta_\infty N(t)$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 Integrating the differential inequality in step 1.2 gives $N(t)\le N(0)+\int_0^t\beta_\infty N(s)\,ds$. Apply [F3] with $a(t)=N(0)$ and $b=\beta_\infty$ to obtain the asserted positive-semigroup bound. [F3, step 1.2, algebra]

2.1 Subtract the two transport equations and write $w=n-\widetilde n$. Along characteristics, its interior forcing is $(\widetilde\mu-\mu)\widetilde n$ and its inflow forcing is $\int\beta w+\int(\beta-\widetilde\beta)\widetilde n$. Taking absolute values in the characteristic integral formula, integrating over age, and using nonnegative survival factors gives $E(t)\le E(0)+\int_0^t[\beta_\infty E(s)+\delta\widetilde N(s)]\,ds$, where $E=\|w\|_1$ and $\widetilde N=\|\widetilde n\|_1$. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 By step 1.3 applied to $\widetilde n$, $\widetilde N(s)\le e^{\widetilde\beta_\infty s}\|\widetilde n_0\|_1$. ## Statement

Under [[def-size-structured-transport-and-division-kernel]], for every initial size $y\in[0,X]$ the extended IVP specified there has a unique solution $\chi_y$ on $[0,T]$. The solution is strictly increasing and agrees with the original growth field until it first reaches $X$, so its restriction through that first hit is the model characteristic.

For [[alg-size-structured-finite-volume-flux-and-kernel-quadrature]], assume nonnegative initial masses, nonnegative quadrature coefficients $A_{j\ell}$, and the stated CFL. Then all $M_j^k$ remain nonnegative. Define the cell number and center-weighted size moment by $N_h^k=\sum_jM_j^k$ and $W_h^k=\sum_jx_j^cM_j^k$. With $k_{0,\ell}^h=\sum_jA_{j\ell}$ and $k_{1,\ell}^h=\sum_jx_j^cA_{j\ell}$, the exact balances are

$$N_h^{k+1}-N_h^k=\Delta t\left(-F_J^k-\sum_jd_jM_j^k+\sum_\ell k_{0,\ell}^hM_\ell^k\right),$$

$$W_h^{k+1}-W_h^k=\Delta t\left(\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}(x_{j+1}^c-x_j^c)F_j^k-x_J^cF_J^k-\sum_jx_j^cd_jM_j^k+\sum_\ell k_{1,\ell}^hM_\ell^k\right).$$

Thus a division kernel preserves the discrete size moment only when its first-moment production cancels the parent-removal term; this identity is not automatic for an arbitrary kernel.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The fixed-interval size model and finite-volume update in [[def-size-structured-transport-and-division-kernel]] and [[alg-size-structured-finite-volume-flux-and-kernel-quadrature]].

[F1] [[def-size-structured-transport-and-division-kernel]]: the total loss rate is $d=\mu+\gamma$, and each daughter kernel is a nonnegative measure supported on sizes no larger than its parent.

[F2] [[alg-size-structured-finite-volume-flux-and-kernel-quadrature]]: the update is $M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j-F_{j-1})-\Delta t d_jM_j^k+\Delta t\sum_\ell A_{j\ell}M_\ell^k$, with nonnegative $A_{j\ell}$ and the stated CFL.

[F3] [[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: a continuous vector field that is locally Lipschitz in the state variable has a unique local IVP solution; its quantitative clause gives a solution on any centered cylinder where the boundedness and contraction conditions hold, and its uniqueness clause applies on common intervals.

[A1] The initial cell masses are nonnegative.

## Proof

1.1 In [F2], the coefficient of $M_j^k$ outside the division source is $1-\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)$, which is nonnegative by the CFL. For $j\ge2$ the incoming transport term has coefficient $\Delta t g(x_{j-1})/h_{j-1}\ge0$; for $j=1$ the incoming flux is $F_0=0$. Every division term has coefficient $\Delta t A_{j\ell}\ge0$. Hence each new mass is a sum of nonnegative terms when [A1] holds. Induction on $k$ proves $M_j^k\ge0$. [A1, F1, F2, induction, algebra]

2.1 Sum [F2] over $j$. The finite flux sum telescopes to $F_J-F_0=F_J$ because $F_0=0$. Interchanging the finite sums in the kernel source gives $\sum_\ell(\sum_jA_{j\ell})M_\ell=\sum_\ell k_{0,\ell}^hM_\ell$. Subtracting $N_h^k$ yields the number identity. [F2, algebra]

2.2 Multiply [F2] by $x_j^c$ and sum over $j$. For the flux term, finite summation by parts gives $\sum_jx_j^c(F_j-F_{j-1})=x_J^cF_J-\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}(x_{j+1}^c-x_j^c)F_j$ since $F_0=0$. The loss term is $-\sum_jx_j^cd_jM_j$, and the source term is $\sum_\ell(\sum_jx_j^cA_{j\ell})M_\ell=\sum_\ell k_{1,\ell}^hM_\ell$. Rearranging proves the weighted-moment identity and the stated condition for cancellation. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $M=\|g\|_\infty$ and let $L$ be a Lipschitz constant for $g$ on $[0,X]$. The projection $\Pi_{[0,X]}$ is $1$-Lipschitz, so the extension $\widetilde g=g\circ\Pi_{[0,X]}$ is globally bounded by $M$ and globally Lipschitz with constant $L$ on the open domain $\mathbb R$. Since $g\ge g_{\min}>0$, choose $h_0>0$ with $h_0M\le1$ and $Lh_0<1$. For every starting time $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and state $z\in\mathbb R$, the cylinder $[t_0-h_0,t_0+h_0]\times[z-1,z+1]$ lies in $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$, and [F3] gives a unique solution through $(t_0,z)$ on that interval; the same bounds apply after every restart. Restricting and concatenating at most $\lceil T/h_0\rceil$ such forward segments gives a solution on $[0,T]$, and the uniqueness clause of [F3] makes it unique there. Along this solution $\chi_y'(s)=\widetilde g(\chi_y(s))\ge g_{\min}$, so it is strictly increasing. Starting from $y\in[0,X]$, it stays in $[0,X]$ through its first hitting of $X$, where $\widetilde g=g$; that restricted segment is the model characteristic. [F1, F3, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-model]], define $K(a)=\beta(a)S(0,a)$ and

$$G_A(t)=\int_0^{A-t}\beta(x+t)S(x,t)n_0^A(x)\,dx,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$

There is a unique continuous nonnegative birth rate satisfying

$$B_A(t)=G_A(t)+\int_0^tK(a)B_A(t-a)\,da,$$

and the finite-age density is, for almost every $0<a<A$,

$$n^A(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0^A(a-t)S(a-t,t),&t\le a<A,\\B_A(t-a)S(0,a),&0\le a<t.\end{cases}$$

It is the unique mild solution, has $B_A(t)=\int_0^A\beta(a)n^A(t,a)\,da$, and obeys

$$\|n^A(t,\cdot)\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty t}\|n_0^A\|_1,\qquad \beta_\infty=\|\beta\|_\infty.$$

For $t\le T<A$, its exact cumulative number outflow is

$$O_A(t)=\int_{A-t}^{A}n_0^A(x)S(x,A-x)\,dx.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Bounded nonnegative Lipschitz rates, $n_0^A\in L^1_+(0,A)$, and the characteristic survival law in [[def-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-model]].

[F1] [[def-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-model]]: characteristics have age $a+s$ and survival $S(a,s)=\exp(-\int_a^{a+s}\mu)$; age $A$ is absorbing outflow, and the birth rate integrates $\beta n^A$ only over $[0,A]$.

[F2] [[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]: if $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_0^t b(s)u(s)\,ds$ with nonnegative continuous $u,b$ and nondecreasing $a$, then $u(t)\le a(t)e^{\int_0^t b}$.

## Proof

1.1 The kernel $K$ is continuous on $[0,T]$. The moving-limit forcing $G_A$ is also continuous: on the common part of the integration intervals its integrand changes uniformly continuously with $t$, and the integral over the symmetric difference tends to zero by absolute continuity of the integral of $n_0^A$. It is nonnegative. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 On any interval of length $\delta$ with $\delta\|K\|_\infty<1$, the map $b\mapsto G_A(t)+\int_0^tK(a)b(t-a)da$ is a contraction on the unknown continuous birth-rate segment, with contraction factor at most $\delta\|K\|_\infty$ after the already determined history is placed in the forcing. If $K=0$, the equation reduces to $B_A=G_A$. Finitely many such intervals cover $[0,T]$, and at each endpoint the defining equation fixes the same value from either adjacent interval; this constructs a unique continuous solution. Picard iteration from zero on each interval preserves nonnegativity because $G_A,K\ge0$, so $B_A\ge0$. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Substitute the displayed density formula into $\int_0^A\beta(a)n^A(t,a)da$. On the initial-cohort part $t\le a<A$, use $x=a-t$ to obtain $G_A(t)$. On the newborn part $0\le a<t$, the integral is $\int_0^t\beta(a)S(0,a)B_A(t-a)da=\int_0^tK(a)B_A(t-a)da$. The Volterra equation therefore gives exactly the renewal boundary relation. Both parts are nonnegative and have finite $L^1$ mass, bounded by $\|n_0^A\|_1+\int_0^tB_A(s)ds$. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Integrating the two characteristic branches gives $N_A(t)=\int_0^{A-t}n_0^A(x)S(x,t)dx+\int_0^tB_A(t-a)S(0,a)da$. This mass function is absolutely continuous; the moving-limit rule and $\partial_tS(x,t)=-\mu(x+t)S(x,t)$ show for almost every $t$ that $N_A'(t)=B_A(t)-\int_0^A\mu(a)n^A(t,a)da-n_0^A(A-t)S(A-t,t)$. The final term is nonnegative outflow, so $N_A'(t)\le B_A(t)\le\beta_\infty N_A(t)$. Integrating and applying [F2] yields $N_A(t)\le e^{\beta_\infty t}N_A(0)$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 For $t\le T<A$, newborn cohorts have age at most $T$ and cannot reach $A$. An initial cohort with age $x$ exits by time $t$ precisely when $A-t\le x<A$; it survives until exit by $S(x,A-x)$. Integrating its initial density over those ages gives the stated $O_A(t)$. Any mild solution must follow these same characteristics and its birth rate must solve the Volterra equation from step 2.1, whose solution is unique by step 1.2. Thus the density and outflow are unique. Translation continuity in $L^1$, continuity of $B_A$ and of $S$, and the vanishing measure of the newly entering cohort region give continuity of $n^A$ in time with values in $L^1(0,A)$. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎
