$$\langle x,y\rangle_B:=y^*Bx,$$
the **B-norm** by
$$\|x\|_B:=\|L^*x\|_2=\sqrt{x^*Bx},$$
and the **B-dual residual norm** by
$$\|r\|_{B^{-1}}:=\|L^{-1}r\|_2 =\sqrt{r^*B^{-1}r}.$$
The B-orthogonality condition is $x^*By=0$; since $B=B^*$ it is equivalent
to $\langle x,y\rangle_B=0$.

Let $A=A^*$ and let $B=B^*$ be positive definite in
$\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, where $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
If $B=LL^*$ is its Cholesky factorisation, then
$$C=L^{-1}AL^{-*}$$
is self-adjoint and has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$. The vectors
$$x_i=L^{-*}y_i\quad (i=1,\ldots,n)$$
form a basis satisfying $Ax_i=\lambda_iBx_i$ and
$x_i^*Bx_j=\delta_{ij}$. The generalized eigenvalues of $(A,B)$ are exactly
$[\lambda_i:1]$; none is infinite.

before.claim: Decompose a B-unit x∈S as u+e with u=P_Ux and e∈U^{⊥_B}. The B-orthonormal eigenbasis diagonalizes the Rayleigh quotient; cross terms vanish, yielding the convex weighted upper bound λ_q+(λ_n−λ_q)||e||_B².
The largest Ritz value is the maximum Rayleigh quotient on S, so 1.1 gives the upper enclosure; L1 gives every lower bound. The strict gap makes the direct sum of the first q eigenspaces unique.

after.claim: By [F2], write a B-unit vector $x\in S$ as $x=u+e$ with $u=P_Ux\in U$ and $e=(I-P_U)x\in U^{\perp_B}$. In the B-orthonormal generalized eigenbasis, if $x=\sum_i a_i u_i$, then $x^*Bx=\sum_i|a_i|^2$ and $x^*Ax=\sum_i\lambda_i|a_i|^2$. Thus $u^*Au\le\lambda_q u^*Bu$ and $e^*Ae\le\lambda_n e^*Be$; the cross terms vanish since $u_i^*Au_j=\lambda_j u_i^*Bu_j=0$ for $i\le q<j$. Therefore $x^*Ax/x^*Bx\le\lambda_q\|u\|_B^2+\lambda_n\|e\|_B^2=\lambda_q+(\lambda_n-\lambda_q)\|e\|_B^2$, which is at most the stated angle bound.

Diagonalizing the finite Hermitian compression shows that $\theta_q(S)$ is the maximum Rayleigh quotient on $S$, so step 1.1 gives its upper bound. The lower bounds $\lambda_j\le\theta_j(S)$ are [L1]. The strict gap isolates the first q eigenspaces, so their sum is unique; no step asserts an iteration rate.

after.quote:
Let $A=A^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $B=B^*>0$, and let
$T=T^*>0$ be a fixed preconditioning operator. Here $B>0$ and $T>0$ mean
$x^*Bx>0$ and $x^*Tx>0$ for every nonzero $x$. The $B$-inner product and
norm are those of [[def-b-inner-product-and-dual-norm-for-definite-pencil]].
Choose a block width $1\le q\le n$, a residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a finite
iteration budget $N_{\max}\ge0$, and an initial matrix $X_0$ with
$X_0^*BX_0=I_q$. The output is a block of Ritz pairs and one of
`converged`, `budget-exhausted`, `rank-loss`, or `invalid-initial-block`.

1. If $X_0$ does not have full column rank or does not satisfy
   $X_0^*BX_0=I_q$, return `invalid-initial-block`. Compute the Rayleigh-Ritz eigenpairs in
   $\operatorname{range}(X_0)$, sorted increasingly, and let $\Theta_0$ be the
   diagonal matrix of the $q$ Ritz values. Set the previous search block
   $D_0$ empty and initialize the iteration counter $k=0$.

2. At iteration $k$, form the original residual block
   $R_k=AX_k-BX_k\Theta_k$. If every column has Euclidean norm at most
   $\tau$, return `converged`. If $k=N_{\max}$, return
   `budget-exhausted` with $(\Theta_k,X_k)$.

3. Compute the preconditioned residual block $W_k=TR_k$ and set
   $Y_k=[X_k,W_k,D_k]$, omitting the empty block at $k=0$. Compute an exact
   rank-revealing $B$-QR with column pivoting as follows. Starting with no
   columns in $Q_k$, for each remaining column $y_j$ of $Y_k$ compute its
   residual $c_j=y_j-Q_k(Q_k^*By_j)$ and choose a column with largest
   $B$-norm $\|c_j\|_B$ (break ties by original column order). If the largest
   residual norm is zero, stop; otherwise append the normalized residual to
   $Q_k$ and remove that pivot column. Let $s_k$ be the number of columns
   appended and let $\Pi_k$ record the pivot order followed by the unused
   columns. If $s_k<q$, return `rank-loss` with the current Ritz pairs; no
   projected solve is attempted on that branch. Otherwise set
   $$S_k=Q_k^*BY_k\Pi_k(:,1:s_k).$$
   The pivot construction gives
   $$Y_k\Pi_k(:,1:s_k)=Q_kS_k,\qquad Q_k^*BQ_k=I_{s_k},$$
   and $S_k$ is invertible because its selected columns are independent.
   Dependent trial columns are discarded and their count is recorded as a
   rank-compression diagnostic.

4. The projected matrix $Q_k^*AQ_k$ is Hermitian, hence normal, so its
   orthonormal eigenbasis and real eigenvalues are supplied by
   [[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]. Solve
   $Q_k^*AQ_kZ_k=Z_k\Theta_{k+1}$ and choose its $q$ smallest eigenvalues. Set
   $C_k=\Pi_k(:,1:s_k)S_k^{-1}Z_k$; then $Y_kC_k=Q_kZ_k$. Partition
   $C_k=\begin{bmatrix}C_X\\C_W\\C_D\end{bmatrix}$, omitting the $C_D$
   block when $D_k$ is empty. The projected metric is positive definite
   because for nonzero $z$, $(Q_kz)^*B(Q_kz)=\|z\|_2^2>0$. Set
   $$X_{k+1}=X_kC_X+W_kC_W+D_kC_D,\qquad D_{k+1}=W_kC_W+D_kC_D,$$
   again omitting the empty-block term. Let $\Theta_{k+1}$ be the selected
   diagonal Ritz-value matrix and increment $k$.

5. Repeat from step 2. No convergence, rate, or accuracy is asserted when the
   budget or rank-loss branch is returned. The exact SPD conditions on $B$ and
   $T$ define the permitted metric and preconditioner; no particular
   incomplete-factorization procedure is assumed.

Let $A=A^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $B=B^*>0$, and let
$T=T^*>0$ be a fixed preconditioning operator. Here $B>0$ and $T>0$ mean
$x^*Bx>0$ and $x^*Tx>0$ for every nonzero $x$. The $B$-inner product and
norm are those of [[def-b-inner-product-and-dual-norm-for-definite-pencil]].
Choose a block width $1\le q\le n$, a residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a finite
iteration budget $N_{\max}\ge0$, and an initial matrix $X_0$ with
$X_0^*BX_0=I_q$. The output is a block of Ritz pairs and one of
`converged`, `budget-exhausted`, `rank-loss`, or `invalid-initial-block`.

1. If $X_0$ does not have full column rank or does not satisfy
   $X_0^*BX_0=I_q$, return `invalid-initial-block`. Compute the Rayleigh-Ritz eigenpairs in
   $\operatorname{range}(X_0)$, sorted increasingly, and let $\Theta_0$ be the
   diagonal matrix of the $q$ Ritz values. Set the previous search block
   $D_0$ empty and initialize the iteration counter $k=0$.

2. At iteration $k$, form the original residual block
   $R_k=AX_k-BX_k\Theta_k$. If every column has Euclidean norm at most
   $\tau$, return `converged`. If $k=N_{\max}$, return
   `budget-exhausted` with $(\Theta_k,X_k)$.

3. Compute the preconditioned residual block $W_k=TR_k$ and set
   $Y_k=[X_k,W_k,D_k]$, omitting the empty block at $k=0$. Compute an exact
   rank-revealing $B$-QR with column pivoting as follows. Starting with no
   columns in $Q_k$, for each remaining column $y_j$ of $Y_k$ compute its
   residual $c_j=y_j-Q_k(Q_k^*By_j)$ and choose a column with largest
   $B$-norm $\|c_j\|_B$ (break ties by original column order). If the largest
   residual norm is zero, stop; otherwise append the normalized residual to
   $Q_k$ and remove that pivot column. Let $s_k$ be the number of columns
   appended and let $\Pi_k$ record the pivot order followed by the unused
   columns. If $s_k<q$, return `rank-loss` with the current Ritz pairs; no
   projected solve is attempted on that branch. Otherwise set
   $$S_k=Q_k^*BY_k\Pi_k(:,1:s_k).$$

   $$Y_k\Pi_k(:,1:s_k)=Q_kS_k,\qquad Q_k^*BQ_k=I_{s_k},$$
   and $S_k$ is invertible because its selected columns are independent.
   Dependent trial columns are discarded and their count is recorded as a
   rank-compression diagnostic.

   orthonormal eigenbasis and real eigenvalues are supplied by

$r_W$ be its exact rank. If $r_W<k$, choose $z\ne0$ with $Wz=0$. Then
$z^*G=(Wz)^*W=0$ and $z^*C=(Wz)^*U=0$. Thus the nonzero row
$z^*$ annihilates $G-\eta C$ for every $\eta$; if this matrix were invertible,
right multiplication by its inverse would force $z^*=0$, a contradiction.
Hence $G-\eta C$ is singular for every $\eta$; return
`projected-pencil-unresolved`. If $W$ has full column rank, then
$z^*Gz=\|Wz\|_2^2>0$ for every $z\ne0$. Thus $G$ is positive definite and
the pencil $G-\eta C$ is regular in the convention of
[[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]], since
$\det(G-0C)=\det G\ne0$.

Supply a finite QZ sweep budget $N\ge0$ and tolerance $\tau_{QZ}\ge0$, and run
[[alg-finite-budget-qz-iteration-with-deflation-and-residual]] on $(G,C)$.
Compute $G,C$ exactly in the mathematical procedure; a finite implementation
must include their formation errors in the perturbation ledger or return
`qz-certificate-inconclusive`. On `qz-computed`, require its exact-factor and
local-update certificates;
[[prop-finite-budget-qz-iteration-terminates-and-preserves-pencil-equivalence]]
then records equivalence to a perturbed projected pencil. For each diagonal
index $i$, set $\alpha_i=S_{ii}$ and $\beta_i=T_{ii}$. If
$(\alpha_i,\beta_i)=(0,0)$, return `projected-pencil-unresolved`; if
$\beta_i\ne0$, report the computed harmonic Ritz value
$\lambda_i=\sigma+\alpha_i/\beta_i$; if $\beta_i=0$, mark that candidate
`infinite-harmonic-value`. These are values of the computed perturbed
pencil, with the QZ residual and perturbation ledger retained; no exact-root,
eigenvector, or forward-error claim is made. Map a QZ `budget-exhausted` status
to `qz-budget-exhausted`; map a QZ `certificate-inconclusive` or `range-failure`
to `qz-certificate-inconclusive`; map `singular-pencil-suspected` to

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, choose a shift
$\sigma\in\mathbb C$, and put $M=A-\sigma I$. This procedure returns candidate
values and their residual data; it asserts no convergence or forward-error
bound. Its branch statuses are `available`, `arnoldi-breakdown`,
`linear-solve-unavailable`, `zero-transformed-Ritz-value`,
`infinite-harmonic-value`, `projected-pencil-unresolved`,
`qz-budget-exhausted`, and `qz-certificate-inconclusive`.

**Shift-invert branch.** This branch requires $M$ to be invertible, equivalently
that $\sigma$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$ by
[[prop-eigenvalue-iff-shift-is-not-invertible]]. Its inputs also include a
nonzero starting vector $v$, an integer Arnoldi dimension $1\le m\le n$, a
residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and a solve routine. Normalize

$y_j=M^{-1}v_j$ or a computed vector $y_j$ together with its actual equation
residual $s_j=My_j-v_j$. If a requested solve is unavailable, return
`linear-solve-unavailable` with the residuals already recorded. Set $w=y_j$.
For $i=1,\ldots,j$, compute $h_{ij}=\langle w,v_i\rangle$ and replace

coefficient to the corresponding $h_{ij}$. Set $h_{j+1,j}=\|w\|_2$. If this
norm is zero, set the current dimension to $k=j$ and stop with status
`arnoldi-breakdown`; otherwise set $v_{j+1}=w/h_{j+1,j}$. After $m$ columns,
set $k=m$ and stop with status `available`.
When every solve is exact, this is Arnoldi applied to $M^{-1}$. When any solve
is inexact, the projected matrix is only the one produced from the computed
vectors; the procedure makes no exact-Arnoldi or convergence claim for that
branch.

Compute the Ritz pairs $(\theta,z)$ of the current $k\times k$ matrix $H$ as
in [[def-ritz-values-and-ritz-vectors-from-arnoldi]], normalize $z$ to unit
norm, and lift $u=V_kz$. For each $\theta\ne0$, report the transformed candidate
$\lambda=\sigma+1/\theta$, the lifted vector $u$, and the directly computed
original residual $r_A=Au-\lambda u$. Mark this candidate accepted exactly
when $\|r_A\|_2\le\tau$. If $\theta=0$, assign no finite inverse map and mark
that candidate `zero-transformed-Ritz-value`. To record the solve-error
transfer for a candidate with $\theta\ne0$, request one additional solve
$My=u$; if it is available, store $s_0=My-u$ and $r_T=y-\theta u$ alongside
the directly computed residual $r_A$.
If this additional solve is unavailable, return
`linear-solve-unavailable` with the candidate and accumulated ledger.

$U\in\mathbb C^{n\times k}$, $k\ge1$; it does not require $M$ to be
invertible. Form $W=MU$ and

Supply a finite QZ sweep budget $N\ge0$ and tolerance $\tau_{QZ}\ge0$, and run

Compute $G,C$ exactly in the mathematical procedure; a finite implementation

then records equivalence to a perturbed projected pencil. For each diagonal
index $i$, set $\alpha_i=S_{ii}$ and $\beta_i=T_{ii}$. If

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $\sigma\in\mathbb C$, and
$M=A-\sigma I$ be invertible. Then a nonzero vector $u$ is an eigenvector of
$A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ if and only if it is an eigenvector of
$M^{-1}$ with eigenvalue $\theta=(\lambda-\sigma)^{-1}$. In particular,
$\lambda=\sigma+1/\theta$ and $\theta\ne0$.

For any nonzero candidate $u$, any $\theta\ne0$, and any computed vector $y$
with solve residual $s_0=My-u$, define the transformed residual
$r_T=y-\theta u$ and $\lambda=\sigma+1/\theta$. Then
$$ (A-\lambda I)u=\theta^{-1}(s_0-Mr_T), $$
and consequently
$$\|(A-\lambda I)u\|_2\le\frac{\|s_0\|_2+\|Mr_T\|_2}{|\theta|}.$$

before.claim: For thick or implicit restarted Arnoldi, one cycle has at most $m$ Arnoldi steps. The thick restart processes finite matrices and blocks, while the implicit restart uses exactly $p=m-r$ shifts and finite QR steps; [A1] makes all invoked rules and projected eigensolves finite-return. Thus each cycle either returns a listed status or reaches its single restart-counter update.

For block LOBPCG, every pass through steps 1--4 is finite: its trial block has finitely many columns, its $B$-orthogonalization processes at most those columns, and the projected eigensolve and finite-dimensional operations return in finite work by [A1]. A pass either returns a status or completes one update and increments $k$.

The counter begins at $0$ and increases by one before each further cycle. After at most $N_{\max}$ such increments, the next completed cycle reaches the test $c=N_{\max}$ and returns `budget-exhausted` unless an earlier acceptance or breakdown status has already returned. The number of cycles is therefore at most $N_{\max}+1$, so the Arnoldi execution terminates.

Starting from $k=0$, no more than $N_{\max}$ updates can occur. After those updates the next pass tests $k=N_{\max}$ and returns `budget-exhausted`, unless convergence or rank loss already returned. Hence the block LOBPCG execution terminates after finitely many operations.

before.quote:
Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $v\ne0$, and choose integers
$1\le r<m\le n$, a residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a restart budget
$N_{\max}\ge1$, a target rule, and a restart mode `thick` or `implicit`.
All operations below are in exact arithmetic. In thick mode, the target rule
selects $r-k$ linearly independent current Ritz vectors, where $k$ denotes
the number of already locked pairs; if it cannot do so, the procedure returns
`rank-loss`. In implicit
mode, a shift rule supplies exactly $p=m-r$ complex shifts for the current
cycle, or reports that the shift list is unavailable. The shifts may be chosen
from unwanted Ritz values, but the procedure allows any supplied list and
asserts no convergence for an arbitrary schedule. Initialize the restart
counter $c=0$ before the first Arnoldi cycle. A cycle consists of expanding
the current Arnoldi basis to dimension $m$ or exact breakdown, then computing
Ritz pairs and testing their original residuals. After the initial cycle in
step 1, each restart in step 3 or 4 constructs the next cycle. The output is
the locked Ritz pairs, the current unlocked Ritz pairs, and one of `converged`,
`budget-exhausted`, `invariant-subspace-breakdown`, `rank-loss`,
`shift-count-unavailable`, or `filtered-breakdown`.

1. Start with $v_1=v/\|v\|_2$, no locked pairs, and run fully reorthogonalized
   Arnoldi to dimension $m$, stopping earlier if the next Arnoldi residual is
   zero. Normalize every nonzero projected eigenvector $y$ so $\|y\|_2=1$ and
   lift it to $u=V_my$. For each Ritz pair $(\theta,u)$, compute the original
   residual $r_u=Au-\theta u$ (on a standard Arnoldi cycle it may be evaluated
   by [[prop-ritz-residual-formula-for-an-arnoldi-ritz-pair]]) and accept the
   pair when $\|r_u\|_2\le\tau$. Accepted pairs are recorded as locked outputs
   and their vectors must be retained at every later restart. If at least $r$
   pairs have been accepted, return `converged`.

2. If the projected Arnoldi space is exactly invariant and fewer than $r$ pairs
   have been accepted, return `invariant-subspace-breakdown`. If the restart
   counter satisfies $c=N_{\max}$, return `budget-exhausted`.

3. For a thick restart, form a target block from every locked vector and the
   additional wanted Ritz vectors selected by the target rule. Apply exact
   exact column-pivoted QR as in
   [[def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations]] to
   this block; if its rank is too small to retain all
   locked and selected directions, return `rank-loss`. With the resulting
   orthonormal basis $U$, compute the residual block
   $R_U=(I-UU^*)AU$. Apply exact column-pivoted QR as in
   [[def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations]] to
   $R_U$, breaking pivot
   ties by original column order, to obtain an ordered orthonormal basis $F$ of
   its range. If $U$ has $q$ columns, retain only the first
   $\min(\dim\operatorname{range}(R_U),m-q)$ columns of $F$, so $[U,F]$ has at
   most $m$ columns. Restart from $[U,F]$ and extend by block Arnoldi, fully
   reorthogonalizing each new $Aq$ against all current columns, until the basis
   has dimension $m$ or the exact residual vanishes. If the retained subspace
   is invariant before dimension $m$ and fewer than $r$ pairs are accepted,
   return `invariant-subspace-breakdown`.

4. For an implicit restart, use this branch only when no pair is locked. Set
   $p=m-r$ and request a shift list $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_p$ from the shift rule;
   if it reports a list of the wrong length, return `shift-count-unavailable`.
   Starting from $AV_m=V_mH_m+\beta_m v_{m+1}e_m^*$, apply exact shifted QR
   steps to $H_m$ using the Givens transformations of
   [[def-real-and-complex-givens-transformations]] in top-down adjacent-row
   eliminations on pairs
   $(1,2),(2,3),\ldots,(m-1,m)$:
   $H_{j-1}-\mu_jI=Q_jR_j$ and $H_j=Q_j^*H_{j-1}Q_j=R_jQ_j+\mu_jI$.
   Put $Q=Q_1\cdots Q_p$, rotate $V_m$ by $Q$, retain its first $r$ columns,
   and continue Arnoldi to dimension $m$. If the polynomial
   $q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^p(z-\mu_j)$ annihilates the starting vector or the
   filtered Krylov space has dimension below $r$, return `filtered-breakdown`.

5. Increment the restart counter by setting $c\gets c+1$, recompute Ritz
   pairs and their original residuals, apply the acceptance rule in step 1,
   and return to step 2 unless a return status applies.
   No convergence is asserted for an arbitrary shift schedule. The residual
   acceptance test certifies only the computed residual size; it does not by
   itself give a forward eigenvalue bound for a nonnormal matrix.

Let $A=A^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $B=B^*>0$, and let
$T=T^*>0$ be a fixed preconditioning operator. Here $B>0$ and $T>0$ mean
$x^*Bx>0$ and $x^*Tx>0$ for every nonzero $x$. The $B$-inner product and
norm are those of [[def-b-inner-product-and-dual-norm-for-definite-pencil]].
Choose a block width $1\le q\le n$, a residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a finite
iteration budget $N_{\max}\ge0$, and an initial matrix $X_0$ with
$X_0^*BX_0=I_q$. The output is a block of Ritz pairs and one of
`converged`, `budget-exhausted`, `rank-loss`, or `invalid-initial-block`.

1. If $X_0$ does not have full column rank or does not satisfy
   $X_0^*BX_0=I_q$, return `invalid-initial-block`. Compute the Rayleigh-Ritz eigenpairs in
   $\operatorname{range}(X_0)$, sorted increasingly, and let $\Theta_0$ be the
   diagonal matrix of the $q$ Ritz values. Set the previous search block
   $D_0$ empty and initialize the iteration counter $k=0$.

2. At iteration $k$, form the original residual block
   $R_k=AX_k-BX_k\Theta_k$. If every column has Euclidean norm at most
   $\tau$, return `converged`. If $k=N_{\max}$, return
   `budget-exhausted` with $(\Theta_k,X_k)$.

3. Compute the preconditioned residual block $W_k=TR_k$ and set
   $Y_k=[X_k,W_k,D_k]$, omitting the empty block at $k=0$. Compute an exact
   rank-revealing $B$-QR with column pivoting as follows. Starting with no
   columns in $Q_k$, for each remaining column $y_j$ of $Y_k$ compute its
   residual $c_j=y_j-Q_k(Q_k^*By_j)$ and choose a column with largest
   $B$-norm $\|c_j\|_B$ (break ties by original column order). If the largest
   residual norm is zero, stop; otherwise append the normalized residual to
   $Q_k$ and remove that pivot column. Let $s_k$ be the number of columns
   appended and let $\Pi_k$ record the pivot order followed by the unused
   columns. If $s_k<q$, return `rank-loss` with the current Ritz pairs; no
   projected solve is attempted on that branch. Otherwise set
   $$S_k=Q_k^*BY_k\Pi_k(:,1:s_k).$$
   The pivot construction gives
   $$Y_k\Pi_k(:,1:s_k)=Q_kS_k,\qquad Q_k^*BQ_k=I_{s_k},$$
   and $S_k$ is invertible because its selected columns are independent.
   Dependent trial columns are discarded and their count is recorded as a
   rank-compression diagnostic.

4. The projected matrix $Q_k^*AQ_k$ is Hermitian, hence normal, so its
   orthonormal eigenbasis and real eigenvalues are supplied by
   [[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]. Solve
   $Q_k^*AQ_kZ_k=Z_k\Theta_{k+1}$ and choose its $q$ smallest eigenvalues. Set
   $C_k=\Pi_k(:,1:s_k)S_k^{-1}Z_k$; then $Y_kC_k=Q_kZ_k$. Partition
   $C_k=\begin{bmatrix}C_X\\C_W\\C_D\end{bmatrix}$, omitting the $C_D$
   block when $D_k$ is empty. The projected metric is positive definite
   because for nonzero $z$, $(Q_kz)^*B(Q_kz)=\|z\|_2^2>0$. Set
   $$X_{k+1}=X_kC_X+W_kC_W+D_kC_D,\qquad D_{k+1}=W_kC_W+D_kC_D,$$
   again omitting the empty-block term. Let $\Theta_{k+1}$ be the selected
   diagonal Ritz-value matrix and increment $k$.

5. Repeat from step 2. No convergence, rate, or accuracy is asserted when the
   budget or rank-loss branch is returned. The exact SPD conditions on $B$ and
   $T$ define the permitted metric and preconditioner; no particular
   incomplete-factorization procedure is assumed.

after.quote:
Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $v\ne0$, and choose integers
$1\le r<m\le n$, a residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a restart budget
$N_{\max}\ge1$, and a restart mode `thick` or `implicit`. All operations
below are in exact arithmetic. The number $k$ of locked pairs is the number
of linearly independent locked vectors; it starts at zero. If a restart is
needed, a target rule may be supplied for thick mode and is required for an
implicit-mode restart after one or more pairs are locked. When invoked, it
must return $r-k$ current Ritz vectors independent modulo the span of all
locked vectors, or report `unavailable`; no rule, an unavailable selection,
or a wrong-size or dependent selection gives status `rank-loss`. For an implicit-mode
restart with no locked pairs, a shift rule supplies exactly $p=m-r$ complex
shifts for the current cycle or reports `unavailable`; an unavailable list or
a list of any other length gives status `shift-count-unavailable`. The shifts
may be chosen from unwanted Ritz values, but the procedure allows any
supplied list and asserts no convergence for an arbitrary schedule.

Initialize the restart counter $c=0$ before the first Arnoldi cycle. A cycle
consists of expanding the current Arnoldi basis to dimension $m$ or exact
breakdown, then computing Ritz pairs and testing their original residuals.
After the initial cycle in step 1, each restart in step 3 or 4 constructs the
next cycle. The output is the locked Ritz pairs, the current unlocked Ritz
pairs, and one of `converged`, `budget-exhausted`,
`invariant-subspace-breakdown`, `rank-loss`, `shift-count-unavailable`, or
`filtered-breakdown`.

1. Start with $v_1=v/\|v\|_2$, no locked pairs, and run fully reorthogonalized
   Arnoldi to dimension $m$, stopping earlier if the next Arnoldi residual is
   zero. Let $d$ be the number of basis columns actually constructed, so
   $d=m$ unless exact breakdown occurs earlier, and let $V_d,H_d$ be the
   resulting basis and projected matrix. Normalize every nonzero projected
   eigenvector $y$ of $H_d$ so $\|y\|_2=1$ and lift it to $u=V_dy$. Process
   the Ritz pairs in the order returned by the projected eigensolve. For each
   pair $(\theta,u)$, compute the original residual $r_u=Au-\theta u$
   directly (on a standard Arnoldi cycle without breakdown it may be
   evaluated by [[prop-ritz-residual-formula-for-an-arnoldi-ritz-pair]]).
   If $\|r_u\|_2\le\tau$ and adding $u$ increases the exact rank of the
   locked-vector matrix, append $(\theta,u)$ to the locked outputs and
   increment $k$. A
   residual-accepted vector in the span of the locked vectors is not counted
   or appended again. Locked vectors are retained as a subspace at every
   later restart. If $k\ge r$, return `converged`.

2. If the projected Arnoldi space is exactly invariant and fewer than $r$
   pairs are locked, return `invariant-subspace-breakdown`. If the restart
   counter satisfies $c=N_{\max}$, return `budget-exhausted`.

3. For a thick restart, or for an implicit-mode restart when $k>0$, invoke
   the target rule. Form a target block from every locked vector and the
   selected $r-k$ wanted Ritz vectors. For either block to be rank-revealing,
   use the following exact column-pivoted orthogonalization: start with an
   empty orthonormal block $Q$ and all input columns remaining. For each
   remaining column $y_j$, compute $c_j=y_j-Q(Q^*y_j)$. Choose a column with
   largest $\|c_j\|_2$, breaking ties by original column order. If the largest
   norm is zero, stop; otherwise append $c_j/\|c_j\|_2$ to $Q$ and remove that
   pivot column. The columns appended to $Q$ form an ordered orthonormal basis
   of the input range. Apply this procedure first to the target block; if it
   fails to retain all locked and selected directions, return `rank-loss`.
   With its resulting orthonormal basis $U$, compute the residual block
   $R_U=(I-UU^*)AU$. Apply the same orthogonalization to $R_U$ to obtain an
   ordered orthonormal basis $F$ of its range. If $U$ has $s$ columns, retain
   only the first $\min(\dim\operatorname{range}(R_U),m-s)$ columns of $F$,
   so $[U,F]$ has at most $m$ columns. Set the ordered basis to $[U,F]$ and a
   queue to its columns in order. While the basis has fewer than $m$ columns
   and the queue is nonempty, remove the first queued column $q$, compute
   $w=Aq$, and orthogonalize $w$ against every current basis column in two
   complete passes. If the residual is nonzero, normalize it, append it to
   the basis, and append the new column to the queue; if it is zero, continue
   with the remaining queue. If the queue empties before the basis has
   dimension $m$, the retained subspace is invariant; when fewer than $r$
   pairs are locked, return `invariant-subspace-breakdown`.

4. For an implicit restart with no locked pairs, set $p=m-r$ and request a
   shift list $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_p$ from the shift rule. If it reports
   `unavailable` or returns a list of the wrong length, return
   `shift-count-unavailable`.
   Starting from $AV_m=V_mH_m+\beta_m v_{m+1}e_m^*$, apply exact shifted QR
   steps to $H_m$ using the Givens transformations of
   [[def-real-and-complex-givens-transformations]] in top-down adjacent-row
   eliminations on pairs
   $(1,2),(2,3),\ldots,(m-1,m)$:
   $H_{j-1}-\mu_jI=Q_jR_j$ and $H_j=Q_j^*H_{j-1}Q_j=R_jQ_j+\mu_jI$.
   Put $Q=Q_1\cdots Q_p$, rotate $V_m$ by $Q$, retain its first $r$ columns,
   and continue Arnoldi to dimension $m$. If the polynomial
   $q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^p(z-\mu_j)$ annihilates the starting vector or the
   filtered Krylov space has dimension below $r$, return `filtered-breakdown`.

5. Increment the restart counter by setting $c\gets c+1$, recompute Ritz
   pairs and their original residuals, apply the acceptance rule in step 1,
   and return to step 2 unless a return status applies.
   No convergence is asserted for an arbitrary shift schedule. The residual
   acceptance test certifies only the computed residual size; it does not by
   itself give a forward eigenvalue bound for a nonnormal matrix.

Let $A=A^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $B=B^*>0$, and let
$T=T^*>0$ be a fixed preconditioning operator. Here $B>0$ and $T>0$ mean
$x^*Bx>0$ and $x^*Tx>0$ for every nonzero $x$. The $B$-inner product and
norm are those of [[def-b-inner-product-and-dual-norm-for-definite-pencil]].
Choose a block width $1\le q\le n$, a residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a finite
iteration budget $N_{\max}\ge0$, and an initial matrix $X_0$ with
$X_0^*BX_0=I_q$. The output is a block of Ritz pairs and one of
`converged`, `budget-exhausted`, `rank-loss`, or `invalid-initial-block`.

1. If $X_0$ does not have full column rank or does not satisfy
   $X_0^*BX_0=I_q$, return `invalid-initial-block`. Compute the Rayleigh-Ritz eigenpairs in
   $\operatorname{range}(X_0)$, sorted increasingly, and let $\Theta_0$ be the
   diagonal matrix of the $q$ Ritz values. Set the previous search block
   $D_0$ empty and initialize the iteration counter $k=0$.

2. At iteration $k$, form the original residual block
   $R_k=AX_k-BX_k\Theta_k$. If every column has Euclidean norm at most
   $\tau$, return `converged`. If $k=N_{\max}$, return
   `budget-exhausted` with $(\Theta_k,X_k)$.

3. Compute the preconditioned residual block $W_k=TR_k$ and set
   $Y_k=[X_k,W_k,D_k]$, omitting the empty block at $k=0$. Compute an exact
   rank-revealing $B$-QR with column pivoting as follows. Starting with no
   columns in $Q_k$, for each remaining column $y_j$ of $Y_k$ compute its
   residual $c_j=y_j-Q_k(Q_k^*By_j)$ and choose a column with largest
   $B$-norm $\|c_j\|_B$ (break ties by original column order). If the largest
   residual norm is zero, stop; otherwise append the normalized residual to
   $Q_k$ and remove that pivot column. Let $s_k$ be the number of columns
   appended and let $\Pi_k$ record the pivot order followed by the unused
   columns. If $s_k<q$, return `rank-loss` with the current Ritz pairs; no
   projected solve is attempted on that branch. Otherwise set
   $$S_k=Q_k^*BY_k\Pi_k(:,1:s_k).$$
   The pivot construction gives
   $$Y_k\Pi_k(:,1:s_k)=Q_kS_k,\qquad Q_k^*BQ_k=I_{s_k},$$
   and $S_k$ is invertible because its selected columns are independent.
   Dependent trial columns are discarded and their count is recorded as a
   rank-compression diagnostic.

4. The projected matrix $Q_k^*AQ_k$ is Hermitian, hence normal, so its
   orthonormal eigenbasis and real eigenvalues are supplied by
   [[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]. Solve
   $Q_k^*AQ_kZ_k=Z_k\Theta_{k+1}$ and choose its $q$ smallest eigenvalues. Set
   $C_k=\Pi_k(:,1:s_k)S_k^{-1}Z_k$; then $Y_kC_k=Q_kZ_k$. Partition
   $C_k=\begin{bmatrix}C_X\\C_W\\C_D\end{bmatrix}$, omitting the $C_D$
   block when $D_k$ is empty. The projected metric is positive definite
   because for nonzero $z$, $(Q_kz)^*B(Q_kz)=\|z\|_2^2>0$. Set
   $$X_{k+1}=X_kC_X+W_kC_W+D_kC_D,\qquad D_{k+1}=W_kC_W+D_kC_D,$$
   again omitting the empty-block term. Let $\Theta_{k+1}$ be the selected
   diagonal Ritz-value matrix and increment $k$.

5. Repeat from step 2. No convergence, rate, or accuracy is asserted when the
   budget or rank-loss branch is returned. The exact SPD conditions on $B$ and
   $T$ define the permitted metric and preconditioner; no particular
   incomplete-factorization procedure is assumed.

before.claim: In the shift-invert branch, the Arnoldi loop has exactly $m$ requested solves unless an earlier solve failure or exact breakdown returns. The Ritz extraction has finitely many candidates (at most $m$); each candidate invokes at most one additional solve. By [A1], each such operation and each residual calculation returns in finite work, and every failure branch explicitly returns a listed status. Therefore this branch terminates.

In the harmonic branch, forming $W,G,C$ and computing the rank of $W$ use finite-dimensional operations by [A1]. If the rank is below $k$, the algorithm returns `projected-pencil-unresolved` before QZ. If the rank is $k$, its statement gives a regular projected pencil and calls QZ with the finite budget $N$; [F3, F4] then give a QZ status after finitely many operations under the assumed QZ hypotheses.

After a QZ return, the algorithm maps each possible QZ status to one of its own listed statuses. On `qz-computed`, it inspects only the finitely many diagonal pairs of the finite projected pencil and either returns on an unresolved pair or completes the candidate list. Thus the harmonic branch also terminates, proving the assertion for both branches.

before.claim: In [F2], the coefficient of $M_j^k$ outside the division source is $1-\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)$, which is nonnegative by the CFL. The incoming transport term has coefficient $\Delta t g(x_{j-1})/h_{j-1}\ge0$, and every division term has coefficient $\Delta t A_{j\ell}\ge0$. Hence each new mass is a sum of nonnegative terms when [A1] holds. Induction on $k$ proves $M_j^k\ge0$.

Sum [F2] over $j$. The finite flux sum telescopes to $F_J-F_0=F_J$ because $F_0=0$. Interchanging the finite sums in the kernel source gives $\sum_\ell(\sum_jA_{j\ell})M_\ell=\sum_\ell k_{0,\ell}^hM_\ell$. Subtracting $N_h^k$ yields the number identity.

Multiply [F2] by $x_j^c$ and sum over $j$. For the flux term, finite summation by parts gives $\sum_jx_j^c(F_j-F_{j-1})=x_J^cF_J-\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}(x_{j+1}^c-x_j^c)F_j$ since $F_0=0$. The loss term is $-\sum_jx_j^cd_jM_j$, and the source term is $\sum_\ell(\sum_jx_j^cA_{j\ell})M_\ell=\sum_\ell k_{1,\ell}^hM_\ell$. Rearranging proves the weighted-moment identity and the stated condition for cancellation.

after.claim: In [F2], the coefficient of $M_j^k$ outside the division source is $1-\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)$, which is nonnegative by the CFL. For $j\ge2$ the incoming transport term has coefficient $\Delta t g(x_{j-1})/h_{j-1}\ge0$; for $j=1$ the incoming flux is $F_0=0$. Every division term has coefficient $\Delta t A_{j\ell}\ge0$. Hence each new mass is a sum of nonnegative terms when [A1] holds. Induction on $k$ proves $M_j^k\ge0$.

Sum [F2] over $j$. The finite flux sum telescopes to $F_J-F_0=F_J$ because $F_0=0$. Interchanging the finite sums in the kernel source gives $\sum_\ell(\sum_jA_{j\ell})M_\ell=\sum_\ell k_{0,\ell}^hM_\ell$. Subtracting $N_h^k$ yields the number identity.

Rearranging proves the weighted-moment identity and the stated condition for cancellation.

Let $M=\|g\|_\infty$ and let $L$ be a Lipschitz constant for $g$ on $[0,X]$. The projection $\Pi_{[0,X]}$ is $1$-Lipschitz, so the extension $\widetilde g=g\circ\Pi_{[0,X]}$ is globally bounded by $M$ and globally Lipschitz with constant $L$ on the open domain $\mathbb R$. Since $g\ge g_{\min}>0$, choose $h_0>0$ with $h_0M\le1$ and $Lh_0<1$. For every starting time $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and state $z\in\mathbb R$, the cylinder $[t_0-h_0,t_0+h_0]\times[z-1,z+1]$ lies in $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$, and [F3] gives a unique solution through $(t_0,z)$ on that interval; the same bounds apply after every restart. Restricting and concatenating at most $\lceil T/h_0\rceil$ such forward segments gives a solution on $[0,T]$, and the uniqueness clause of [F3] makes it unique there. Along this solution $\chi_y'(s)=\widetilde g(\chi_y(s))\ge g_{\min}$, so it is strictly increasing. Starting from $y\in[0,X]$, it stays in $[0,X]$ through its first hitting of $X$, where $\widetilde g=g$; that restricted segment is the model characteristic.

before.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a fixed size interval $[0,X]$. Let $g,\mu,\gamma:[0,X]\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded Lipschitz functions, with $g(x)\ge g_{\min}>0$. Here $g$ is size growth, $\mu$ is ordinary mortality, and $\gamma$ is the rate at which a dividing parent is removed. For each parent size $y$, let $K_y$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure of daughter sizes, supported on $[0,y]$. Assume $y\mapsto K_y(E)$ is measurable for every Borel set $E\subseteq[0,X]$, and that the number moment $k_0(y):=K_y([0,y])$ is uniformly bounded; the size moment $k_1(y):=\int_{[0,y]}x\,K_y(dx)$ is then finite. The **size-structured transport and division model** is

$$\partial_t n+\partial_x(gn)=-(\mu+\gamma)n+\int_{[0,X]}K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy,\qquad 0<x<X,$$

with zero incoming flux at $x=0$ and absorbing outflow $g(X)n(t,X)$ at $x=X$. The transport characteristic solves $x'(t)=g(x(t))$ as a first-order IVP in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. The weak equation is obtained by testing against $\phi\in C^1([0,X])$: transport contributes $\int_0^Xg\phi'n$, mortality and parent removal contribute $-\int_0^X(\mu+\gamma)\phi n$, division contributes $\int_0^X\int\phi(x)K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy$, and the upper boundary contributes $-\phi(X)g(X)n(t,X)$. The interval is fixed; moving boundaries, zero growth and discontinuous coefficients are outside this definition.

Partition $[0,X]$ into disjoint cells $C_j=[x_{j-1},x_j)$ for $j<J$ and $C_J=[x_{J-1},X]$, with widths $h_j=x_j-x_{j-1}>0$ and centers $x_j^c=(x_{j-1}+x_j)/2$. Let $M_j^k$ be the mass in cell $C_j$ and $u_j^k=M_j^k/h_j$. Set the incoming flux $F_0^k=0$, the internal and outgoing upwind fluxes $F_j^k=g(x_j)u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$, and $d_j=\mu(x_j^c)+\gamma(x_j^c)$.

For each parent cell $C_\ell$, form nonnegative daughter coefficients

$$A_{j\ell}=\frac{1}{h_\ell}\,Q_M\bigl(y\mapsto K_y(C_j);x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1\bigr),$$

using [[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]] on the parent-size interval. Since the one-panel midpoint rule is $Q_M(f;x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1)=h_\ell f(x_\ell^c)$, this gives $A_{j\ell}=K_{x_\ell^c}(C_j)\ge0$. The finite-volume update is

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,d_jM_j^k+\Delta t\sum_{\ell=1}^JA_{j\ell}M_\ell^k.$$

The flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow. The admissible variable-width CFL is $\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)\le1$ for every cell. If a grid, coefficient evaluation or kernel quadrature fails, the procedure returns an explicit failure status and performs no partial update.

after.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a nondegenerate fixed size interval $[0,X]$ with $X>0$. Let $g,\mu,\gamma:[0,X]\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded Lipschitz functions, with $g(x)\ge g_{\min}>0$. Here $g$ is size growth, $\mu$ is ordinary mortality, and $\gamma$ is the rate at which a dividing parent is removed. For each parent size $y$, let $K_y$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure of daughter sizes, supported on $[0,y]$. Assume $y\mapsto K_y(E)$ is measurable for every Borel set $E\subseteq[0,X]$, and that the number moment $k_0(y):=K_y([0,y])$ is uniformly bounded; the size moment $k_1(y):=\int_{[0,y]}x\,K_y(dx)$ is then finite. The **size-structured transport and division model** is

$$\partial_t n+\partial_x(gn)=-(\mu+\gamma)n+\int_{[0,X]}K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy,\qquad 0<x<X,$$

with zero incoming flux at $x=0$ and absorbing outflow $g(X)n(t,X)$ at $x=X$. Let $\Pi_{[0,X]}(x):=\min\{X,\max\{0,x\}\}$ and extend the growth field to $\widetilde g(x):=g(\Pi_{[0,X]}(x))$ on $\mathbb R$. This is a bounded Lipschitz vector field. By [[thm-size-structured-positivity-number-and-weighted-moment-identities]], its IVP has a unique solution on the finite time horizon; a model characteristic is this solution restricted to the interval from its initial size until its first hitting of $X$, including that hitting time when it occurs by $T$. On this restricted interval, $\widetilde g=g$. The characteristic is understood as a first-order IVP solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. The weak equation is obtained by testing against $\phi\in C^1([0,X])$: transport contributes $\int_0^Xg\phi'n$, mortality and parent removal contribute $-\int_0^X(\mu+\gamma)\phi n$, division contributes $\int_0^X\int\phi(x)K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy$, and the upper boundary contributes $-\phi(X)g(X)n(t,X)$. The interval is fixed; moving boundaries, zero growth and discontinuous coefficients are outside this definition.

Input a partition $0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_J=X$ with $J\ge1$, a time step $\Delta t>0$, a nonnegative current mass vector $M^k=(M_j^k)_{j=1}^J$, and the coefficients and kernel from [[def-size-structured-transport-and-division-kernel]]. Partition $[0,X]$ into disjoint cells $C_j=[x_{j-1},x_j)$ for $j<J$ and $C_J=[x_{J-1},X]$, with widths $h_j=x_j-x_{j-1}>0$ and centers $x_j^c=(x_{j-1}+x_j)/2$. Set $u_j^k=M_j^k/h_j$, the incoming flux $F_0^k=0$, the internal and outgoing upwind fluxes $F_j^k=g(x_j)u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$, and $d_j=\mu(x_j^c)+\gamma(x_j^c)$.

For each parent cell $C_\ell$, form nonnegative daughter coefficients

$$A_{j\ell}=\frac{1}{h_\ell}\,Q_M\bigl(y\mapsto K_y(C_j);x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1\bigr),$$

using [[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]] on the parent-size interval. Since the one-panel midpoint rule is $Q_M(f;x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1)=h_\ell f(x_\ell^c)$, this gives $A_{j\ell}=K_{x_\ell^c}(C_j)\ge0$. If $\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)>1$ for any cell, return `invalid-cfl` without an update. Otherwise the finite-volume update is

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,d_jM_j^k+\Delta t\sum_{\ell=1}^JA_{j\ell}M_\ell^k.$$

The flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow. The admissible variable-width CFL is $\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)\le1$ for every cell. If a grid or any required coefficient/kernel evaluation fails, return failure without a partial update. Otherwise return $M^{k+1}$ together with the fluxes and daughter coefficients used in the step.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

before.claim: Let $\widehat n$ be the exact solution with initial density $\widehat n_0$. Applying the characteristic formula [F2] and changing variables from age $a$ to birth time $s=t-a$ gives, for every bounded Lipschitz $\phi$, $\int\phi(a)\widehat n(t,a)da=\int_0^{A-T}\phi(x+t)S(x,t)n_0(x)dx+\int_0^t\phi(t-s)S(0,t-s)\widehat B(s)ds$. The birth kernel $K(s)=\beta(s)S(0,s)$ is bounded and Lipschitz, and $\widehat G(t)=\int_0^{A-T}\beta(x+t)S(x,t)n_0(x)dx$ is bounded and Lipschitz because $\beta,\mu$ have bounded first derivatives and $n_0$ is integrable. The mass estimate [F5] bounds $\widehat B$ by $\beta_\infty e^{\beta_\infty T}\|n_0\|_1$. Subtracting its Volterra equation at $t$ and $t+h$, the old-history kernel difference is at most $\operatorname{Lip}(K)h\int_0^T|\widehat B|$ and the new interval at most $h\|K\|_\infty\|\widehat B\|_\infty$. Thus $\widehat B$ is Lipschitz on $[0,T]$.

A cohort born with mass $m_0$ and initial age $a_0$ has exact survival mass solving $m'(s)=-\mu(a_0+s)m(s)$. The vector field $f(s,m)=-\mu(a_0+s)m$ is $C^1$ on $0\le s\le T$, $0\le m\le m_0$, with derivative bounds independent of $a_0$ because $\mu,\mu'$ are globally bounded. By [F4], one Euler step has defect at most $C\Delta t^2m_0$ and stability factor $1+L\Delta t$; iterating the recurrence over at most $T/\Delta t$ steps gives survival-weight error at most $C_T\Delta t m_0$. For the discrete total cohort mass $N_h^k$, positivity and $B_h^k\le\beta_\infty N_h^k$ give $N_h^{k+1}\le(1+\Delta t\beta_\infty)N_h^k$, hence $N_h^k\le e^{\beta_\infty T}N_h^0$. Since $N_h^0\le\|n_0\|_1+\epsilon_0$ (test the initial BL defect with $\phi\equiv1$), the sum of the initial cohort masses and all inserted newborn masses $\sum_{j<k}\Delta t B_h^j$ is at most $C_T(\|n_0\|_1+\epsilon_0)$. Thus the sum of all cohort survival-weight errors is at most $C_T\Delta t(\|n_0\|_1+\epsilon_0)$.

Write $e_k=|B_h^k-\widehat B(t_k)|$. before.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $T>0$. Let mortality and fertility be bounded Lipschitz functions $\mu,\beta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, and let $n_0\in L^1(0,\infty)$ be nonnegative. The **linear age-structured renewal transport problem** is

$$n_t(t,a)+n_a(t,a)=-\mu(a)n(t,a),\qquad a>0,\quad 0<t\le T,$$

with initial density $n(0,a)=n_0(a)$ and inflow condition

$$n(t,0)=B(t),\qquad B(t):=\int_0^\infty \beta(a)n(t,a)\,da.$$

Here $a$ is age, $B$ is the birth rate, and the characteristic age path solves the first-order initial value problem $a'(s)=1$ in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], hence $a(s)=a(0)+s$. Define survival from age $a$ over duration $s\ge0$ by

$$S(a,s):=\exp\!\left(-\int_a^{a+s}\mu(r)\,dr\right).$$

A **weak solution** on $[0,T]$ is a nonnegative $n\in C([0,T];L^1(0,\infty))$ with continuous $B:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$ and, for every $\phi\in C_c^1([0,T]\times[0,\infty))$ with $\phi(T,a)=0$,

$$-\int_0^T\!\int_0^\infty n(t,a)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu(a)\phi)\,da\,dt=\int_0^\infty n_0(a)\phi(0,a)\,da+\int_0^T B(t)\phi(t,0)\,dt.$$

A **mild solution** is a weak solution that also satisfies, for almost every $a\ge0$,

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)S(a-t,t),&a\ge t,\\B(t-a)S(0,a),&0\le a<t,\end{cases}$$

The formula follows the age characteristics $a'(s)=1$ and their mortality survival. No delay equation or finite-age cutoff is identified with this model by definition.

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], put $M(a)=\int_0^a\mu(r)\,dr$, $K(a)=\beta(a)e^{-M(a)}$, and

$$G(t)=\int_0^\infty \beta(x+t)\exp\!\left(-\int_x^{x+t}\mu(r)\,dr\right)n_0(x)\,dx.$$

There is a unique mild solution. Its birth rate is the unique continuous solution of

$$B(t)=G(t)+\int_0^t K(a)B(t-a)\,da,$$

and its density, for almost every $a\ge0$, is

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)\exp\!\left(-\int_{a-t}^{a}\mu(r)\,dr\right),&a\ge t,\\ B(t-a)e^{-M(a)},&0\le a<t.\end{cases}$$

Input a finite time step $\Delta t$, an age cutoff $A$, nonnegative rates $\mu,\beta$ on $[0,A]$, and a finite positive initial quadrature $(a_i,m_i^0)_{i=1}^I$ supported in $[0,A)$ for the initial age measure on that interval. One option is the composite midpoint rule on a partition of $[0,A]$: for each panel midpoint $a_i$, set $m_i^0=\Delta a\,n_0(a_i)$. A cohort at age $a_i^k$ and mass $m_i^k$ follows the exact age characteristic

$$a_i^{k+1}=a_i^k+\Delta t$$

and updates its survival mass by forward Euler,

$$m_i^{k+1}=(1-\Delta t\,\mu(a_i^k))m_i^k.$$

At time $t_k$, calculate the finite cohort birth rate $B_h^k=\sum_i\beta(a_i^k)m_i^k$. Advance each existing cohort's age by $\Delta t$ and update its survival mass by the displayed Euler step. If its updated age is at least $A$, record that updated mass as discrete outflow and discard the cohort; otherwise retain it. Then insert a newborn cohort of age $0$ and mass $\Delta t B_h^k$ at time $t_{k+1}$. Require $\Delta t\|\mu\|_\infty\le1$. A failed rate evaluation returns failure. The procedure returns the finite positive measure $\nu_h^k=\sum_i m_i^k\delta_{a_i^k}$ and its birth/outflow records. The bounded-Lipschitz quadrature defect of the initial measure and the Euler survival error are separate inputs to any consistency claim.

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be an open time-state domain whose fibers $V_t:=\{z:(t,z)\in V\}$ are open and convex. Let $K\subset V$ be compact. Let $f:V\to\mathbb R^d$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and suppose $y$ is a solution of $y'=f(t,y)$, $y(0)=y_0$, on an open interval containing $[0,T]$, with graph on $[0,T]$ contained in $K$. For each local defect under consideration, require the Euler input and output time-state pairs to lie in $K$; the exact solution segment already lies in $K$.

For $1\le i,j\le d$, assume finite constants $F_j,M_{t,i},M_{ij},L\ge0$ satisfy throughout $V$

$$|f_j(t,z)|\le F_j,\qquad |\partial_t f_i(t,z)|\le M_{t,i},\qquad |\partial_{z_j}f_i(t,z)|\le M_{ij},\qquad \|D_yf(t,z)w\|_2\le L\|w\|_2\quad(w\in\mathbb R^d).$$

Here $D_yf$ is the matrix with entries $\partial_{z_j}f_i$, and the last inequality defines the operator bound used below. The forward Euler map is $\Psi_h(t,v)=v+h f(t,v)$. Then, with $B_i:=M_{t,i}+\sum_{j=1}^dM_{ij}F_j$, for every $t\in[0,T)$ and $h>0$ with $t+h\le T$ whose Euler input and output pairs lie in $K$, its local defect satisfies

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le \frac{h^2}{2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^d B_i^2\right)^{1/2},$$

so it has uniform local order one on $K$ along $y|_{[0,T]}$, with $h_0=T$. For every $t\in[0,T]$, every admitted $h>0$, and every $u,v\in V_t$,

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2.$$

This is a local defect and one-step stability result. It does not assert a global error estimate or an order for any other named method.

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], let $\beta_\infty=\|\beta\|_\infty$. The solution map $S_{\mu,\beta}(t):n_0\mapsto n(t,\cdot)$ is linear and positive, and

$$\|S_{\mu,\beta}(t)n_0\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty t}\|n_0\|_1.$$

If $n,\widetilde n$ use possibly different nonnegative bounded coefficients $(\mu,\beta)$ and $(\widetilde\mu,\widetilde\beta)$ and initial data $n_0,\widetilde n_0$, put $\delta=\|\mu-\widetilde\mu\|_\infty+\|\beta-\widetilde\beta\|_\infty$ and $\widetilde\beta_\infty=\|\widetilde\beta\|_\infty$. Then

$$\|n(t)-\widetilde n(t)\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty t}\left(\|n_0-\widetilde n_0\|_1+\delta t e^{\widetilde\beta_\infty t}\|\widetilde n_0\|_1\right).$$

Let $T>0$, $N\ge1$, $h=T/N$, $p\ge1$, and $C_0,C,L\ge0$. If nonnegative real numbers $e_0,\ldots,e_N$ satisfy
$$e_0\le C_0h^p,\qquad e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+Ch^{p+1}\quad(0\le n<N),$$
then, when $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, when $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

before.claim: Substituting $F_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$ in [F2] gives $M_1^{k+1}=(1-\lambda-\Delta t\mu_1)M_1^k+\Delta t B_h^k$ and, for $j\ge2$, $M_j^{k+1}=(1-\lambda-\Delta t\mu_j)M_j^k+\lambda M_{j-1}^k$. The CFL makes every displayed coefficient nonnegative, while [F1] makes $B_h^k\ge0$; induction in $k$ proves nonnegativity.

Summing [F2] over cells telescopes the fluxes to $F_J^k-F_0^k$, hence $N_h^{k+1}=N_h^k-\Delta t F_J^k+\Delta t B_h^k-\Delta t\sum_j\mu_jM_j^k$. Since $F_J^k,\mu_j,M_j^k\ge0$ and [F1] gives $B_h^k\le\beta_\infty N_h^k$, the asserted mass-growth inequality follows.

The update is a linear matrix with nonnegative entries by step 1.1. In each column, transport and mortality leave total coefficient at most $1$, because outflow or mortality removes mass; the birth quadrature adds at most $\Delta t\beta_\infty$ to that column by [F1]. Thus its induced $\ell^1$ norm is at most $1+\Delta t\beta_\infty$. Applying this matrix to $M^k-\widetilde M^k$ proves the difference estimate.

after.claim: In midpoint mode, each of the $q_j$ samples has weight $\Delta a/q_j>0$, so the weights sum to the cell width. In capped-adaptive mode, every returned estimate is a finite sum of Simpson panel estimates on its leaf intervals; a two-panel Simpson block has weights proportional to $(1,4,1)$, all positive, and their sum is the block width. The leaf intervals partition the cell, so the combined weights are nonnegative and sum to its width, including when a cap is reached. Hence the cell contribution lies between $0$ and $u_j\beta_\infty\Delta a=\beta_\infty M_j$, and summing over cells gives the stated birth bound. A failure returns no estimate.

Substituting $F_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$ in [F2] gives $M_1^{k+1}=(1-\lambda-\Delta t\mu_1)M_1^k+\Delta t B_h^k$ and, for $j\ge2$, $M_j^{k+1}=(1-\lambda-\Delta t\mu_j)M_j^k+\lambda M_{j-1}^k$. For each $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, put $u_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$, compute $B_h^k$ with [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]], and set the upwind fluxes $F_0^k=B_h^k$ and $F_j^k=u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$. Update, for $1\le j\le J$,

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,\mu_jM_j^k.$$

The right flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow: record and discard the step mass $\Delta t F_J^k$, set $O_h^{k+1}=O_h^k+\Delta t F_J^k$, and allow no inflow from ages above $A$. Append $B_h^k$, the quadrature status, and the step outflow record, then proceed to step $k+1$. Return $(M^k)_{k=0}^N$ with the birth, quadrature-status, step-outflow, and cumulative-outflow records. An invalid grid or failed rate/quadrature evaluation returns failure with no partial current step. A `cap-reached` adaptive quadrature estimate may be used for a finite step, but its status is retained and carries no accuracy claim.

For the bounded fertility rate in the age model, write $\beta_\infty:=\|\beta\|_\infty$. Whenever [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]] returns an estimate for nonnegative cell masses and a bounded nonnegative fertility rate with upper bound $\beta_\infty$, its birth value satisfies $0\le B_h\le\beta_\infty\sum_jM_j$.

$$\|M^{k+1}-\widetilde M^{k+1}\|_{\ell^1}\le(1+\Delta t\,\beta_\infty)\|M^k-\widetilde M^k\|_{\ell^1}.$$

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$. Let mortality and fertility be bounded Lipschitz functions $\mu,\beta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, and let $n_0\in L^1(0,\infty)$ be nonnegative. The **linear age-structured renewal transport problem** is

$$n_t(t,a)+n_a(t,a)=-\mu(a)n(t,a),\qquad a>0,\quad 0<t\le T,$$

with initial density $n(0,a)=n_0(a)$ and inflow condition

$$n(t,0)=B(t),\qquad B(t):=\int_0^\infty \beta(a)n(t,a)\,da.$$

Here $a$ is age, $B$ is the birth rate, and the characteristic age path solves the first-order initial value problem $a'(s)=1$ in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], hence $a(s)=a(0)+s$. Define survival from age $a$ over duration $s\ge0$ by

$$S(a,s):=\exp\!\left(-\int_a^{a+s}\mu(r)\,dr\right).$$

A **weak solution** on $[0,T]$ is a nonnegative $n\in C([0,T];L^1(0,\infty))$ with continuous $B:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$ and, for every $\phi\in C_c^1([0,T]\times[0,\infty))$ with $\phi(T,a)=0$,

$$-\int_0^T\!\int_0^\infty n(t,a)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu(a)\phi)\,da\,dt=\int_0^\infty n_0(a)\phi(0,a)\,da+\int_0^T B(t)\phi(t,0)\,dt.$$

A **mild solution** is a weak solution that also satisfies, for almost every $a\ge0$,

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)S(a-t,t),&a\ge t,\\B(t-a)S(0,a),&0\le a<t,\end{cases}$$

The formula follows the age characteristics $a'(s)=1$ and their mortality survival. No delay equation or finite-age cutoff is identified with this model by definition.

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], put $M(a)=\int_0^a\mu(r)\,dr$, $K(a)=\beta(a)e^{-M(a)}$, and

$$G(t)=\int_0^\infty \beta(x+t)\exp\!\left(-\int_x^{x+t}\mu(r)\,dr\right)n_0(x)\,dx.$$

There is a unique mild solution. Its birth rate is the unique continuous solution of

$$B(t)=G(t)+\int_0^t K(a)B(t-a)\,da,$$

and its density, for almost every $a\ge0$, is

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)\exp\!\left(-\int_{a-t}^{a}\mu(r)\,dr\right),&a\ge t,\\ B(t-a)e^{-M(a)},&0\le a<t.\end{cases}$$

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-model]], define $K(a)=\beta(a)S(0,a)$ and

$$G_A(t)=\int_0^{A-t}\beta(x+t)S(x,t)n_0^A(x)\,dx,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$

There is a unique continuous nonnegative birth rate satisfying

$$B_A(t)=G_A(t)+\int_0^tK(a)B_A(t-a)\,da,$$

and the finite-age density is, for almost every $0<a<A$,

$$n^A(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0^A(a-t)S(a-t,t),&t\le a<A,\\B_A(t-a)S(0,a),&0\le a<t.\end{cases}$$

It is the unique mild solution, has $B_A(t)=\int_0^A\beta(a)n^A(t,a)\,da$, and obeys

$$\|n^A(t,\cdot)\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty t}\|n_0^A\|_1,\qquad \beta_\infty=\|\beta\|_\infty.$$

For $t\le T<A$, its exact cumulative number outflow is

$$O_A(t)=\int_{A-t}^{A}n_0^A(x)S(x,A-x)\,dx.$$

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], let $\beta_\infty=\|\beta\|_\infty$. The solution map $S_{\mu,\beta}(t):n_0\mapsto n(t,\cdot)$ is linear and positive, and

$$\|S_{\mu,\beta}(t)n_0\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty t}\|n_0\|_1.$$

If $n,\widetilde n$ use possibly different nonnegative bounded coefficients $(\mu,\beta)$ and $(\widetilde\mu,\widetilde\beta)$ and initial data $n_0,\widetilde n_0$, put $\delta=\|\mu-\widetilde\mu\|_\infty+\|\beta-\widetilde\beta\|_\infty$ and $\widetilde\beta_\infty=\|\widetilde\beta\|_\infty$. Then

$$\|n(t)-\widetilde n(t)\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty t}\left(\|n_0-\widetilde n_0\|_1+\delta t e^{\widetilde\beta_\infty t}\|\widetilde n_0\|_1\right).$$

Fix $T>0$ and a cutoff $A>T$. Let $n^A$ be the finite-age solution from [[thm-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-characteristic-solution]] with initial density $n_0^A\in C^2([0,A])$ and assume $\mu,\beta\in C^2([0,A])$ are nonnegative and bounded. Assume $n^A$ extends to $C^2([0,T]\times[0,A])$. Its smoothness at the renewal corner includes $n_0^A(0)=B_A(0)$ and $-(n_0^A)'(0)-\mu(0)n_0^A(0)=B_A'(0)$; no boundary value is imposed at the absorbing outflow. Use exact initial cell masses, the one-panel midpoint rule in each cell from [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]], and a mesh with $\Delta t/\Delta a\in[c_-,c_+]$ for fixed $0<c_-\le c_+<\infty$, satisfying the transport-plus-loss CFL. Define

$$\epsilon_Q:=\max_{0\le k<N}\left|B_h(\overline M(t_k))-\int_0^A\beta(a)n^A(t_k,a)\,da\right|,$$

where $B_h(\overline M(t_k))$ is the birth-rate quadrature applied to the exact cell-average masses $\overline M_j(t_k)=\int_{C_j}n^A(t_k,a)\,da$. Then the cell-mass error $E_k=\sum_j|M_j^k-\int_{C_j}n^A(t_k,a)\,da|$ obeys

before.claim: The parent center $2$ lies in the third cell and its daughters have size $1$, exactly the second cell center. Thus the positive midpoint kernel quadrature gives $A_{2,3}=2$ and all other daughter coefficients for the occupied parent column vanish. The CFL number is $0.1(0.1/0.5+1)=0.12$ in cell 1 and $0.1(0.1/1+1)=0.11$ in each of cells 2–4, so the global maximum is $0.12\le1$.

The parent outflow flux is $F_3=gM_3/h_3=0.3$, the daughter source is $\Delta t A_{2,3}M_3=0.6$, and parent removal is $\Delta t\gamma M_3=0.3$. Therefore the updated cell masses are $M_2'=0.6$, $M_3'=3-0.03-0.3=2.67$, and $M_4'=0.03$, with $M_1'=0$; they are all nonnegative.

The discrete number changes from $3$ to $0.6+2.67+0.03=3.3$, an increase $0.3$ equal to $\Delta t(2-1)\gamma M_3$. The weighted-size total changes from $2\cdot3=6$ to $1\cdot0.6+2\cdot2.67+3\cdot0.03=6.03$. Formula [F3] gives the same $0.03$ increase from transport, while division contributes $\Delta t(2\cdot1-2\cdot1)M_3=0$. Thus the first moment is conserved by division and changes only by the size-growth flux in this step.

before.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a fixed size interval $[0,X]$. Let $g,\mu,\gamma:[0,X]\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded Lipschitz functions, with $g(x)\ge g_{\min}>0$. Here $g$ is size growth, $\mu$ is ordinary mortality, and $\gamma$ is the rate at which a dividing parent is removed. For each parent size $y$, let $K_y$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure of daughter sizes, supported on $[0,y]$. Assume $y\mapsto K_y(E)$ is measurable for every Borel set $E\subseteq[0,X]$, and that the number moment $k_0(y):=K_y([0,y])$ is uniformly bounded; the size moment $k_1(y):=\int_{[0,y]}x\,K_y(dx)$ is then finite. The **size-structured transport and division model** is

$$\partial_t n+\partial_x(gn)=-(\mu+\gamma)n+\int_{[0,X]}K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy,\qquad 0<x<X,$$

with zero incoming flux at $x=0$ and absorbing outflow $g(X)n(t,X)$ at $x=X$. The transport characteristic solves $x'(t)=g(x(t))$ as a first-order IVP in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. The weak equation is obtained by testing against $\phi\in C^1([0,X])$: transport contributes $\int_0^Xg\phi'n$, mortality and parent removal contribute $-\int_0^X(\mu+\gamma)\phi n$, division contributes $\int_0^X\int\phi(x)K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy$, and the upper boundary contributes $-\phi(X)g(X)n(t,X)$. The interval is fixed; moving boundaries, zero growth and discontinuous coefficients are outside this definition.

Partition $[0,X]$ into disjoint cells $C_j=[x_{j-1},x_j)$ for $j<J$ and $C_J=[x_{J-1},X]$, with widths $h_j=x_j-x_{j-1}>0$ and centers $x_j^c=(x_{j-1}+x_j)/2$. Let $M_j^k$ be the mass in cell $C_j$ and $u_j^k=M_j^k/h_j$. Set the incoming flux $F_0^k=0$, the internal and outgoing upwind fluxes $F_j^k=g(x_j)u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$, and $d_j=\mu(x_j^c)+\gamma(x_j^c)$.

For each parent cell $C_\ell$, form nonnegative daughter coefficients

$$A_{j\ell}=\frac{1}{h_\ell}\,Q_M\bigl(y\mapsto K_y(C_j);x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1\bigr),$$

using [[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]] on the parent-size interval. Since the one-panel midpoint rule is $Q_M(f;x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1)=h_\ell f(x_\ell^c)$, this gives $A_{j\ell}=K_{x_\ell^c}(C_j)\ge0$. The finite-volume update is

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,d_jM_j^k+\Delta t\sum_{\ell=1}^JA_{j\ell}M_\ell^k.$$

The flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow. The admissible variable-width CFL is $\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)\le1$ for every cell. If a grid, coefficient evaluation or kernel quadrature fails, the procedure returns an explicit failure status and performs no partial update.

For [[alg-size-structured-finite-volume-flux-and-kernel-quadrature]], assume nonnegative initial masses, nonnegative quadrature coefficients $A_{j\ell}$, and the stated CFL. Then all $M_j^k$ remain nonnegative. Define the cell number and center-weighted size moment by $N_h^k=\sum_jM_j^k$ and $W_h^k=\sum_jx_j^cM_j^k$. With $k_{0,\ell}^h=\sum_jA_{j\ell}$ and $k_{1,\ell}^h=\sum_jx_j^cA_{j\ell}$, the exact balances are

$$N_h^{k+1}-N_h^k=\Delta t\left(-F_J^k-\sum_jd_jM_j^k+\sum_\ell k_{0,\ell}^hM_\ell^k\right),$$

$$W_h^{k+1}-W_h^k=\Delta t\left(\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}(x_{j+1}^c-x_j^c)F_j^k-x_J^cF_J^k-\sum_jx_j^cd_jM_j^k+\sum_\ell k_{1,\ell}^hM_\ell^k\right).$$

Thus a division kernel preserves the discrete size moment only when its first-moment production cancels the parent-removal term; this identity is not automatic for an arbitrary kernel.

after.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a nondegenerate fixed size interval $[0,X]$ with $X>0$. Let $g,\mu,\gamma:[0,X]\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded Lipschitz functions, with $g(x)\ge g_{\min}>0$. Here $g$ is size growth, $\mu$ is ordinary mortality, and $\gamma$ is the rate at which a dividing parent is removed. For each parent size $y$, let $K_y$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure of daughter sizes, supported on $[0,y]$. Assume $y\mapsto K_y(E)$ is measurable for every Borel set $E\subseteq[0,X]$, and that the number moment $k_0(y):=K_y([0,y])$ is uniformly bounded; the size moment $k_1(y):=\int_{[0,y]}x\,K_y(dx)$ is then finite. The **size-structured transport and division model** is

$$\partial_t n+\partial_x(gn)=-(\mu+\gamma)n+\int_{[0,X]}K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy,\qquad 0<x<X,$$

with zero incoming flux at $x=0$ and absorbing outflow $g(X)n(t,X)$ at $x=X$. Let $\Pi_{[0,X]}(x):=\min\{X,\max\{0,x\}\}$ and extend the growth field to $\widetilde g(x):=g(\Pi_{[0,X]}(x))$ on $\mathbb R$. This is a bounded Lipschitz vector field. By [[thm-size-structured-positivity-number-and-weighted-moment-identities]], its IVP has a unique solution on the finite time horizon; a model characteristic is this solution restricted to the interval from its initial size until its first hitting of $X$, including that hitting time when it occurs by $T$. On this restricted interval, $\widetilde g=g$. The characteristic is understood as a first-order IVP solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. The weak equation is obtained by testing against $\phi\in C^1([0,X])$: transport contributes $\int_0^Xg\phi'n$, mortality and parent removal contribute $-\int_0^X(\mu+\gamma)\phi n$, division contributes $\int_0^X\int\phi(x)K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy$, and the upper boundary contributes $-\phi(X)g(X)n(t,X)$. The interval is fixed; moving boundaries, zero growth and discontinuous coefficients are outside this definition.

Input a partition $0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_J=X$ with $J\ge1$, a time step $\Delta t>0$, a nonnegative current mass vector $M^k=(M_j^k)_{j=1}^J$, and the coefficients and kernel from [[def-size-structured-transport-and-division-kernel]]. Partition $[0,X]$ into disjoint cells $C_j=[x_{j-1},x_j)$ for $j<J$ and $C_J=[x_{J-1},X]$, with widths $h_j=x_j-x_{j-1}>0$ and centers $x_j^c=(x_{j-1}+x_j)/2$. Set $u_j^k=M_j^k/h_j$, the incoming flux $F_0^k=0$, the internal and outgoing upwind fluxes $F_j^k=g(x_j)u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$, and $d_j=\mu(x_j^c)+\gamma(x_j^c)$.

For each parent cell $C_\ell$, form nonnegative daughter coefficients

$$A_{j\ell}=\frac{1}{h_\ell}\,Q_M\bigl(y\mapsto K_y(C_j);x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1\bigr),$$

using [[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]] on the parent-size interval. Since the one-panel midpoint rule is $Q_M(f;x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1)=h_\ell f(x_\ell^c)$, this gives $A_{j\ell}=K_{x_\ell^c}(C_j)\ge0$. If $\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)>1$ for any cell, return `invalid-cfl` without an update. Otherwise the finite-volume update is

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,d_jM_j^k+\Delta t\sum_{\ell=1}^JA_{j\ell}M_\ell^k.$$

The flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow. The admissible variable-width CFL is $\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)\le1$ for every cell. If a grid or any required coefficient/kernel evaluation fails, return failure without a partial update. Otherwise return $M^{k+1}$ together with the fluxes and daughter coefficients used in the step.

Under [[def-size-structured-transport-and-division-kernel]], for every initial size $y\in[0,X]$ the extended IVP specified there has a unique solution $\chi_y$ on $[0,T]$. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$. Let mortality and fertility be bounded Lipschitz functions $\mu,\beta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, and let $n_0\in L^1(0,\infty)$ be nonnegative. The **linear age-structured renewal transport problem** is

$$n_t(t,a)+n_a(t,a)=-\mu(a)n(t,a),\qquad a>0,\quad 0<t\le T,$$

with initial density $n(0,a)=n_0(a)$ and inflow condition

$$n(t,0)=B(t),\qquad B(t):=\int_0^\infty \beta(a)n(t,a)\,da.$$

Here $a$ is age, $B$ is the birth rate, and the characteristic age path solves the first-order initial value problem $a'(s)=1$ in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], hence $a(s)=a(0)+s$. Define survival from age $a$ over duration $s\ge0$ by

$$S(a,s):=\exp\!\left(-\int_a^{a+s}\mu(r)\,dr\right).$$

A **weak solution** on $[0,T]$ is a nonnegative $n\in C([0,T];L^1(0,\infty))$ with continuous $B:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$ and, for every $\phi\in C_c^1([0,T]\times[0,\infty))$ with $\phi(T,a)=0$,

$$-\int_0^T\!\int_0^\infty n(t,a)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu(a)\phi)\,da\,dt=\int_0^\infty n_0(a)\phi(0,a)\,da+\int_0^T B(t)\phi(t,0)\,dt.$$

A **mild solution** is a weak solution that also satisfies, for almost every $a\ge0$,

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)S(a-t,t),&a\ge t,\\B(t-a)S(0,a),&0\le a<t,\end{cases}$$

The formula follows the age characteristics $a'(s)=1$ and their mortality survival. No delay equation or finite-age cutoff is identified with this model by definition.

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], put $M(a)=\int_0^a\mu(r)\,dr$, $K(a)=\beta(a)e^{-M(a)}$, and

$$G(t)=\int_0^\infty \beta(x+t)\exp\!\left(-\int_x^{x+t}\mu(r)\,dr\right)n_0(x)\,dx.$$

There is a unique mild solution. Its birth rate is the unique continuous solution of

$$B(t)=G(t)+\int_0^t K(a)B(t-a)\,da,$$

and its density, for almost every $a\ge0$, is

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)\exp\!\left(-\int_{a-t}^{a}\mu(r)\,dr\right),&a\ge t,\\ B(t-a)e^{-M(a)},&0\le a<t.\end{cases}$$

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], choose a finite cutoff $A>T$, an integer $J\ge1$, and use the uniform grid $a_j=j\Delta a$ with $\Delta a=A/J$ and cells $C_j=[a_{j-1},a_j]$. Given time step $\Delta t=T/N$, initial nonnegative cell masses $M_j^0$, and the values $\mu_j=\mu((a_{j-1}+a_j)/2)$, require the transport-plus-loss CFL

$$\lambda+\Delta t\,\mu_\infty\le1,\qquad \lambda=\Delta t/\Delta a,\quad\mu_\infty=\|\mu\|_\infty.$$

At time $t_k=k\Delta t$, put $u_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$. Compute $B_h^k$ with [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]] and set the upwind fluxes $F_0^k=B_h^k$ and $F_j^k=u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$. Update, for $1\le j\le J$,

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,\mu_jM_j^k.$$

The right flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow: its mass $\Delta t F_J^k$ is recorded and discarded, with no inflow from ages above $A$. Invalid grids or a failed quadrature return explicit failure statuses. A `cap-reached` adaptive quadrature estimate may still be used for a finite step, but its status is retained and carries no accuracy claim.

In the update of [[alg-age-structured-renewal-upwind-finite-volume]], suppose the initial masses are nonnegative, the CFL holds, and each cell quadrature has nonnegative weights summing to $\Delta a$. Then all updated masses remain nonnegative and, with $N_h^k=\sum_{j=1}^J M_j^k$,

$$N_h^{k+1}\le(1+\Delta t\,\beta_\infty)N_h^k.$$

For two runs with the same grid, rates and quadrature rule but different nonnegative initial mass vectors $M^0,\widetilde M^0$, the one-step difference satisfies

$$\|M^{k+1}-\widetilde M^{k+1}\|_{\ell^1}\le(1+\Delta t\,\beta_\infty)\|M^k-\widetilde M^k\|_{\ell^1}.$$
